questions.text: Due to the inert pair effect, which oxidation state is more stable for thallium (Tl)?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the inert pair effect**
The inert pair effect refers to the reluctance of the outermost \( ns^{2} \) electron pair of heavy p-block elements to participate in bonding, because poor shielding by the intervening \( d \) and \( f \) electrons raises the effective nuclear charge felt by the \( ns \) electrons.

**Step 2: Apply this to thallium**
Tl has the configuration \( [Xe]4f^{14}5d^{10}6s^{2}6p^{1} \); the filled \( 4f \) and \( 5d \) shells shield the \( 6s^{2} \) pair poorly, so this pair stays tightly held and non-bonding, favouring loss of only the single \( 6p \) electron.

**Final Answer**
Because the \( 6s^{2} \) pair resists ionization, Tl(I) compounds (e.g. TlCl) are more stable than Tl(III) compounds, unlike the lighter group 13 members where +3 dominates.
Final answer: A) +1
questions.tip: Whenever you see the heaviest member of groups 13-16 (Tl, Pb, Bi), suspect the inert pair effect favouring the oxidation state two units below the group number.

questions.text: Boron shows a well-known diagonal relationship with which element of the periodic table?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the basis of diagonal relationships**
Elements placed diagonally across the periodic table can resemble each other when their charge-to-radius ratio (polarizing power) is similar, even though they belong to different groups.

**Step 2: Compare boron and silicon**
Boron (period 2, group 13) and silicon (period 3, group 14) have comparable size and polarizing power; both form covalent, acidic oxides, behave as semiconductors/metalloids, and form volatile covalent halides that hydrolyse readily, unlike the more metallic aluminium.

**Final Answer**
This diagonal similarity explains why boron chemistry (e.g. covalent character, acidic oxide) is closer to silicon than to its own group neighbour aluminium.
Final answer: B) Silicon
questions.tip: Diagonal relationships in the periodic table always run from a period-2 element to the period-3 element one group to its right.

questions.text: How many three-centre two-electron (3c-2e) bonds are present in diborane, B2H6?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the structure of diborane**
Diborane has 4 terminal B-H bonds, which are normal two-centre two-electron (2c-2e) bonds, and 2 bridging B-H-B bonds connecting the two BH2 units.

**Step 2: Identify the nature of the bridge bonds**
Each bridging bond involves 2 boron atoms and 1 hydrogen atom sharing only 2 electrons among 3 atoms; such an electron-deficient 'banana bond' is called a 3c-2e bond. Diborane contains exactly 2 of these bridge bonds.

**Final Answer**
The presence of 2 three-centre two-electron bonds explains why diborane is described as electron-deficient, since only 12 valence electrons are available for what would normally require 14 for 7 conventional 2c-2e bonds.
Final answer: B) 2
questions.tip: Count terminal bonds as normal 2c-2e and bridge bonds as 3c-2e; diborane always has exactly 4 terminal + 2 bridge bonds.

questions.text: Anhydrous AlCl3 exists as a dimer, Al2Cl6, in the vapour phase. What is the nature of the two bridging bonds that hold the dimer together?
options: Ionic bonds formed by complete electron transfer
Coordinate (dative) bonds formed by lone pairs on bridging Cl donating into vacant orbitals on Al
Metallic bonding between the two Al centres
Hydrogen bonds between Cl and Al
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recognize the electron deficiency of AlCl3**
In monomeric AlCl3, aluminium has only 6 electrons around it (3 Al-Cl bonds), so it is short of an octet and behaves as a strong Lewis acid.

**Step 2: Explain dimer formation**
Each electron-deficient Al accepts a lone pair from a chlorine atom on the neighbouring AlCl3 unit, forming a coordinate bond; two such Cl bridges link the two Al atoms, giving each Al a tetrahedral, octet-satisfied environment in Al2Cl6.

**Final Answer**
This dative bridging is a general strategy electron-deficient trihalides use to satisfy the octet, analogous to bridge bonding seen in boron hydrides.
Final answer: B) Coordinate (dative) bonds formed by lone pairs on bridging Cl donating into vacant orbitals on Al
questions.tip: Remember Al2Cl6 bridges are ordinary coordinate bonds via Cl lone pairs, unlike the electron-deficient 3c-2e bridges in diborane.

questions.text: Boric acid, H3BO3, behaves as a weak monobasic acid in water. What is the correct explanation for this behaviour?
options: It directly releases H+ ions from all three O-H groups
It acts as a Lewis acid, accepting OH- from a water molecule and releasing H+ (H3O+), rather than donating a proton itself
It contains only one ionizable hydrogen atom
It is a strong protonic (Bronsted) triprotic acid
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the structure of boric acid**
H3BO3 is a planar molecule, B(OH)3, in which boron is \( sp^{2} \) hybridized with only 6 electrons around it, making it electron deficient and a good Lewis acid.

**Step 2: Explain its acidic behaviour**
Instead of donating a proton from an O-H bond, boron accepts a pair of electrons from the OH- of a water molecule, forming \( [B(OH)_{4}]^{-} \) and liberating \( H^{+} \) (as \( H_{3}O^{+} \)): \[ B(OH)_{3} + 2H_{2}O \rightarrow [B(OH)_{4}]^{-} + H_{3}O^{+} \]

**Final Answer**
Because only one H+ is released per molecule via this Lewis-acid mechanism, boric acid is classified as a weak monobasic acid, not a Bronsted triprotic acid.
Final answer: B) It acts as a Lewis acid, accepting OH- from a water molecule and releasing H+ (H3O+), rather than donating a proton itself
questions.tip: Whenever a p-block hydroxide is described as a 'Lewis acid in water', expect it to generate H+ indirectly by attacking OH- of water, not by classical ionization.

questions.text: Unlike aluminium, boron cannot form an octahedral complex ion such as [BF6]3- analogous to [AlF6]3-. What is the fundamental reason for this?
options: Boron is more electronegative than fluorine
Boron has no vacant d-orbitals in its valence shell, so its maximum covalency is limited to 4
Boron atoms are too large to be surrounded by 6 fluorine atoms
The B-F bond is purely ionic, preventing complex formation
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the valence shell available to boron**
Boron is a period-2 element, so its valence shell contains only \( 2s \) and \( 2p \) orbitals (4 orbitals total); there are no \( 2d \) orbitals available to expand its octet.

**Step 2: Compare with aluminium**
Aluminium is in period 3 and has energetically accessible \( 3d \) orbitals, allowing it to expand its coordination number beyond 4 (e.g. \( [AlF_{6}]^{3-}\)); boron, restricted to 4 orbitals, can form at most 4 bonds, as seen in \( [BF_{4}]^{-} \).

**Final Answer**
This absence of valence d-orbitals is the general reason period-2 elements (B, C, N, O, F) cap their covalency at 4, while their heavier congeners can exceed it.
Final answer: B) Boron has no vacant d-orbitals in its valence shell, so its maximum covalency is limited to 4
questions.tip: Whenever comparing a period-2 element to its heavier group member, check first whether d-orbitals are available in the valence shell — this single fact explains most 'anomalous' maximum-covalency differences.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly represents the trend in first ionization enthalpy across group 13 elements (B, Al, Ga, In, Tl)?
options: B > Al > Ga > In > Tl (smooth decrease)
B > Al < Ga > In < Tl (irregular, zig-zag pattern)
B < Al < Ga < In < Tl (smooth increase)
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Expect the normal group trend**
Ionization enthalpy is generally expected to decrease down a group as atomic size increases and the outer electron is progressively farther from the nucleus.

**Step 2: Identify the irregularity after Al**
Gallium follows a filled \( 3d^{10} \) subshell, which shields the nucleus poorly; the resulting higher effective nuclear charge makes IE(Ga) greater than IE(Al). Similarly, thallium follows filled \( 4f^{14}5d^{10}\) subshells, giving IE(Tl) greater than IE(In).

**Final Answer**
The overall pattern B > Al < Ga > In < Tl reflects the poor shielding by intervening d and f electrons, a recurring anomaly across the post-transition p-block elements.
Final answer: B) B > Al < Ga > In < Tl (irregular, zig-zag pattern)
questions.tip: Whenever d10 or f14 electrons intervene just before a p-block element, expect an unexpected rise in ionization enthalpy relative to the element directly above it.

questions.text: Which group 14 element shows the maximum tendency for catenation (self-linking to form chains)?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall what governs catenation ability**
Catenation depends on the strength of the element-element single bond, which in turn depends on effective orbital overlap; smaller atoms with comparable orbital sizes overlap more efficiently.

**Step 2: Compare bond enthalpies down the group**
The C-C bond enthalpy (about 348 kJ/mol) is the highest in the group; as atomic size increases down the group (Si, Ge, Sn, Pb), the E-E bond becomes progressively longer and weaker, so catenation ability sharply decreases: C >> Si > Ge approximately Sn >> Pb.

**Final Answer**
This exceptional catenation ability of carbon is the structural basis of the vast field of organic chemistry.
Final answer: A) Carbon
questions.tip: Catenation tendency in group 14 always follows C >> Si > Ge, and Pb shows almost none of it.

questions.text: Which allotrope of carbon consists of sp2-hybridized carbon atoms arranged in planar hexagonal sheets, with delocalized pi electrons responsible for its electrical conductivity along the sheet?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall carbon's hybridization options**
Carbon can be \( sp^{3} \) hybridized (tetrahedral, as in diamond) or \( sp^{2} \) hybridized (trigonal planar, as in graphite), with the hybridization determining the resulting network structure.

**Step 2: Connect structure to conductivity**
In graphite, each carbon is \( sp^{2} \) hybridized and bonded to 3 neighbours in a hexagonal sheet, leaving one unhybridized \( p \) orbital per carbon; these overlap to form a delocalized pi electron cloud that can move freely within the plane, making graphite an electrical conductor along the sheets (but not perpendicular to them).

**Final Answer**
This planar, delocalized structure of graphite contrasts with diamond, where all four electrons are localized in strong sigma bonds, making diamond an electrical insulator.
Final answer: B) Graphite
questions.tip: Diamond insulator, graphite conductor: the key difference is sp3 (all bonds localized) versus sp2 with one free delocalized electron per carbon.

questions.text: In pyrosilicate ions, Si2O7^6-, two SiO4 tetrahedra are linked to each other by sharing:
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the basis of silicate classification**
Silicates are classified by how many oxygen corners of the basic SiO4 tetrahedron are shared with neighbouring tetrahedra: 0 (orthosilicates), 1 (pyrosilicates), 2 (chain/ring silicates), 3 (sheet silicates), or 4 (three-dimensional silicates like quartz).

**Step 2: Apply this to the pyrosilicate ion**
Two SiO4 tetrahedra sharing exactly one corner oxygen gives the pyrosilicate unit \( Si_{2}O_{7}^{6-} \), which has 6 terminal oxygens plus 1 shared bridging oxygen, totalling 7 oxygen atoms for 2 silicon atoms.

**Final Answer**
Recognizing the number of shared corners immediately tells you the silicate class and its formula, a key organizing principle for silicate structures.
Final answer: A) One corner (one bridging oxygen atom)
questions.tip: Count shared O per tetrahedron: 0=ortho, 1=pyro, 2=chain/ring, 3=sheet, 4=3-D network — this single count fixes the silicate's formula.

questions.text: Due to the inert pair effect, which of the following is a stronger oxidizing agent, being readily reduced from the +4 to the +2 state?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the inert pair effect trend in group 14**
Down group 14, the +2 oxidation state becomes progressively more stable relative to +4, because the \( ns^{2}\) electron pair (here \( 6s^{2}\) for Pb) becomes increasingly reluctant to participate in bonding.

**Step 2: Apply this to lead's +4 compounds**
Since Pb(II) is more stable than Pb(IV), compounds of Pb in the +4 state, such as \( PbO_{2}\), readily accept electrons and get reduced to the more stable \( Pb^{2+}\) state, making \( PbO_{2}\) a strong oxidizing agent, unlike \( SnO_{2}\) where the +4 state is still reasonably stable.

**Final Answer**
This is a direct consequence of the inert pair effect intensifying down the group, making PbO2 (and PbCl4) much stronger oxidizers than their tin analogues.
Final answer: A) PbO2
questions.tip: Whenever Pb(IV) or Tl(III) or Bi(V) compounds appear as reagents, expect them to be good oxidizing agents due to the inert pair effect favouring the lower oxidation state.

questions.text: Silicone polymers, containing a repeating -O-Si(R2)-O- backbone, are commercially prepared by the hydrolysis and subsequent condensation of which starting material?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the synthesis route**
Alkyl or aryl chlorides are reacted with silicon (Rochow process, using a Cu catalyst) to give a mixture of chlorosilanes \( R_{n}SiCl_{4-n}\); the dialkyldichlorosilane \( R_{2}SiCl_{2}\) is the key monomer used to build linear polymer chains.

**Step 2: Explain the hydrolysis-condensation sequence**
Hydrolysis of \( R_{2}SiCl_{2}\) gives the unstable diol \( R_{2}Si(OH)_{2}\), which undergoes intermolecular condensation, losing water molecules to form long chains with a repeating \( -O-Si(R_{2})-O- \) backbone: this is the silicone polymer.

**Final Answer**
Choosing R3SiCl, R2SiCl2, or RSiCl3 as starting monomers controls whether the resulting silicone is chain-terminating, linear, or cross-linked, respectively.
Final answer: B) Dialkyl/diaryl dichlorosilane, R2SiCl2
questions.tip: Silicone chemistry always starts from chlorosilanes RnSiCl4-n; the number of R groups on Si controls the final polymer's branching.

questions.text: Which statement correctly explains why CO2 is a gas at room temperature made of discrete molecules, while SiO2 is a hard, high-melting solid?
options: Carbon and oxygen (both period 2) have comparable 2p orbital sizes allowing strong pi-pi overlap to form discrete O=C=O molecules held together only by weak van der Waals forces; silicon's larger, more diffuse 3p orbitals cannot achieve effective pi-pi overlap with oxygen's 2p orbitals, so Si instead forms four sigma bonds per atom, building a giant three-dimensional network of SiO4 tetrahedra
CO2 is an ionic compound while SiO2 is fully covalent
The Si-O bond is intrinsically weaker than the C-O bond
CO2 has a much higher molar mass than SiO2, making it more volatile
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the requirement for effective pi-pi bonding**
Strong \( p\pi-p\pi\) bonding between two atoms requires their p orbitals to be of comparable size for good sideways overlap; this works well between two period-2 atoms like C and O.

**Step 2: Contrast carbon and silicon's bonding with oxygen**
Carbon forms two strong \( C=O\) pi bonds giving the linear, discrete \( CO_{2}\) molecule, held in the solid/liquid state only by weak van der Waals forces (hence low melting/boiling point, a gas at room temperature). Silicon's valence \( 3p\) orbitals are too large and diffuse to overlap effectively with oxygen's \( 2p\) orbitals, so silicon instead forms four \( Si-O\) sigma bonds per Si atom, and these SiO4 tetrahedra link at every corner into an infinite covalent lattice.

**Final Answer**
This inability of silicon to form strong pi bonds with oxygen (unlike carbon) is why SiO2 exists as a giant covalent 3-D network (quartz) rather than as a simple molecular gas.
Final answer: A) Carbon and oxygen (both period 2) have comparable 2p orbital sizes allowing strong pi-pi overlap to form discrete O=C=O molecules held together only by weak van der Waals forces; silicon's larger, more diffuse 3p orbitals cannot achieve effective pi-pi overlap with oxygen's 2p orbitals, so Si instead forms four sigma bonds per atom, building a giant three-dimensional network of SiO4 tetrahedra
questions.tip: Whenever comparing a period-2 element's oxide to its period-3 congener's oxide, check pi-bonding ability first — it usually explains the molecular-vs-giant-network structural difference.

questions.text: Consider the following statements about the inert pair effect on group 14 halides: (I) Stability of the +4 oxidation state decreases down the group. (II) PbCl4 is thermally less stable than PbCl2 and decomposes on warming to give PbCl2 and Cl2. Which is correct?
options: Both I and II are correct
Both I and II are incorrect
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the trend in the inert pair effect down group 14**
The inert pair effect strengthens down the group because the \( ns^{2}\) electrons are shielded increasingly poorly by intervening \( d\) and \( f\) electrons, making these electrons progressively less willing to be used in bonding; this reduces the stability of the group oxidation state (+4) relative to the (group - 2) state (+2).

**Step 2: Apply this to lead's chlorides**
Since +2 becomes more stable than +4 for lead, \( PbCl_{4}\) is thermodynamically unstable relative to \( PbCl_{2}\); it decomposes on warming: \[ PbCl_{4} \rightarrow PbCl_{2} + Cl_{2} \] confirming both statement I (general trend) and statement II (specific consequence for lead) are correct.

**Final Answer**
This decomposition of PbCl4 is a textbook illustration of how the inert pair effect makes the highest oxidation state increasingly unstable for the heaviest members of a p-block group.
Final answer: A) Both I and II are correct
questions.tip: Whenever PbX4 or PbO2 appears in a reaction, expect it to behave as an unstable oxidizer that reverts to the +2 state, releasing the halogen or oxygen.

questions.text: Dinitrogen, N2, is chemically inert at room temperature mainly because of:
options: Its very high bond dissociation enthalpy arising from the strong N triple bond N
The large atomic size of nitrogen
Availability of vacant d-orbitals on nitrogen for extra bonding
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the bonding in N2**
Two nitrogen atoms are held together by one sigma and two pi bonds, giving an overall triple bond, \( N \equiv N \), which is short (109.8 pm) and extremely strong.

**Step 2: Connect bond strength to reactivity**
The bond dissociation enthalpy of \( N_{2}\) (about 941 kJ/mol) is one of the highest known for a diatomic molecule; breaking this bond to initiate a reaction requires a very large activation energy, so N2 remains largely unreactive at ordinary temperatures.

**Final Answer**
This extraordinarily strong triple bond is why nitrogen fixation (e.g. in the Haber process) requires high temperature, pressure, and a catalyst.
Final answer: A) Its very high bond dissociation enthalpy arising from the strong N triple bond N
questions.tip: A very high bond dissociation enthalpy is the single most important reason for the chemical inertness of N2 at room temperature.

questions.text: White phosphorus (P4) is far more reactive than red phosphorus. What is the main structural reason for this?
options: The P-P-P bond angle in the tetrahedral P4 molecule is only 60 degrees, causing severe angular strain that makes white phosphorus unstable and reactive
Red phosphorus is molecular while white phosphorus is ionic
White phosphorus contains ionic P-P bonds
Red phosphorus has a smaller bond angle than white phosphorus
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the structure of white phosphorus**
White phosphorus exists as discrete tetrahedral P4 molecules, in which each phosphorus atom is bonded to three others with a bond angle of only 60 degrees, far less than the normal bond angle of about 109.5 degrees expected for a p-orbital-based framework.

**Step 2: Connect strain to reactivity**
This severe angular (bent-bond) strain destabilizes the P-P bonds, making white phosphorus highly reactive; it is pyrophoric (spontaneously catches fire in air) and must be stored under water, unlike the polymeric, less strained red phosphorus, which is far more stable.

**Final Answer**
Recognizing ring/cage strain as the cause of reactivity is a recurring theme in p-block allotrope chemistry (also relevant to strained ring silicates and boranes).
Final answer: A) The P-P-P bond angle in the tetrahedral P4 molecule is only 60 degrees, causing severe angular strain that makes white phosphorus unstable and reactive
questions.tip: White phosphorus's 60-degree bond angles under high strain is the key fact explaining both its reactivity and the need to store it under water.

questions.text: The H-N-H bond angle in NH3 (about 107 degrees) is larger than the H-P-H bond angle in PH3 (about 93.5 degrees). What best explains this difference?
options: Nitrogen is more electronegative than phosphorus, pulling bonding electron density closer to itself and increasing bond pair-bond pair repulsion, which widens the angle; in PH3 the less electronegative P keeps bonding pairs farther away, so bonding uses almost pure p-orbitals with minimal hybridization, keeping the angle close to 90 degrees
Phosphorus has a larger lone pair that causes greater repulsion, widening its bond angle
NH3 is an ionic molecule while PH3 is covalent
PH3 involves d-orbital participation, which increases its bond angle beyond that of NH3
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the electronegativity difference between N and P**
Nitrogen ( electronegativity about 3.0) is considerably more electronegative than phosphorus (about 2.1); a more electronegative central atom pulls the shared bonding electron density closer to itself.

**Step 2: Connect this to bond angle via electron pair repulsion**
In NH3, the bond pairs are drawn closer to N, increasing bond pair-bond pair repulsion and pushing the N-H bonds farther apart (larger angle, closer to tetrahedral). In PH3, the bonding electrons stay farther from the larger, less electronegative P atom, so bond pair-bond pair repulsion is weaker; bonding then occurs using orbitals with little s character (nearly pure p orbitals, which are at 90 degrees), giving PH3 a bond angle much closer to 90 degrees.

**Final Answer**
This trend (bond angle decreasing markedly from NH3 to PH3, AsH3, SbH3) tracks the falling electronegativity of the central atom down group 15.
Final answer: A) Nitrogen is more electronegative than phosphorus, pulling bonding electron density closer to itself and increasing bond pair-bond pair repulsion, which widens the angle; in PH3 the less electronegative P keeps bonding pairs farther away, so bonding uses almost pure p-orbitals with minimal hybridization, keeping the angle close to 90 degrees
questions.tip: Down group 15 hydride bond angles fall steadily toward 90 degrees as the central atom's electronegativity drops and bonding approaches pure p-orbital character.

questions.text: What is the correct order of thermal stability of the group 15 hydrides NH3, PH3, AsH3, SbH3, and BiH3?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Identify the factor governing hydride stability**
Thermal stability of a hydride EH3 depends on the strength of the E-H bond, which in turn depends on the extent of orbital overlap between the central atom and hydrogen's small 1s orbital.

**Step 2: Apply the trend down the group**
As atomic size of the central atom increases down group 15 (N to Bi), the E-H bond becomes progressively longer and the overlap with hydrogen's compact orbital becomes poorer, weakening the bond; hence thermal stability decreases steadily: \( NH_{3} > PH_{3} > AsH_{3} > SbH_{3} > BiH_{3}\).

**Final Answer**
This same size-driven weakening of E-H bonds also explains why the reducing character of these hydrides increases in the reverse order, from NH3 to BiH3.
Final answer: A) NH3 > PH3 > AsH3 > SbH3 > BiH3
questions.tip: For any p-block hydride series, thermal stability always falls down the group because increasing central-atom size weakens orbital overlap with hydrogen.

questions.text: In PCl5, which has a trigonal bipyramidal geometry, the axial P-Cl bonds are experimentally found to be longer than the equatorial P-Cl bonds. What is the reason for this?
options: Each axial bond experiences three 90-degree repulsive interactions from the equatorial bonds, while each equatorial bond experiences only two 90-degree repulsions from axial bonds, so axial bonds are weakened and elongated
Equatorial bonds experience greater lone pair repulsion
Axial and equatorial P-Cl bonds are actually of equal length
Equatorial bonds have less s-character than axial bonds
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the geometry of PCl5**
PCl5 is trigonal bipyramidal ( \( sp^{3}d\) hybridized P), with 3 equatorial chlorines at 120 degrees to each other and 2 axial chlorines perpendicular to the equatorial plane.

**Step 2: Compare repulsions on axial versus equatorial bonds**
An axial bond pair is at 90 degrees to all 3 equatorial bond pairs (3 strong 90-degree repulsions), whereas an equatorial bond pair is at 90 degrees to only the 2 axial bond pairs (2 such repulsions) and at 120 degrees to the other equatorial pairs (weaker repulsion). The greater cumulative repulsion on axial bonds weakens and lengthens them (about 219 pm) compared to the shorter, stronger equatorial bonds (about 204 pm).

**Final Answer**
This axial-versus-equatorial bond length difference in trigonal bipyramidal molecules is a general VSEPR consequence, also seen in other sp3d species.
Final answer: A) Each axial bond experiences three 90-degree repulsive interactions from the equatorial bonds, while each equatorial bond experiences only two 90-degree repulsions from axial bonds, so axial bonds are weakened and elongated
questions.tip: In any trigonal bipyramidal molecule, axial bonds are always longer and weaker than equatorial bonds due to more 90-degree repulsions.

questions.text: In hypophosphorous acid, H3PO2, what are the oxidation state of phosphorus and the basicity of the acid respectively?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Determine the basicity from the structure**
H3PO2 has one P-OH group, two P-H bonds, and one P=O bond. Only hydrogen attached through oxygen (P-O-H) is ionizable in water; P-H bonds are non-polar and non-acidic. With only 1 ionizable P-OH group, H3PO2 is monobasic despite having 3 hydrogen atoms in its formula.

**Step 2: Calculate the oxidation state of phosphorus**
Let the oxidation number of P be x. Using H = +1 (3 H atoms) and O = -2 (2 O atoms) for the neutral molecule: \[ x + 3(+1) + 2(-2) = 0 \] \[ x + 3 - 4 = 0 \Rightarrow x = +1 \]

**Final Answer**
H3PO2 is therefore a monobasic acid with phosphorus in the +1 oxidation state, illustrating that basicity is fixed by ionizable P-OH groups, not by the total hydrogen count.
Final answer: A) +1, monobasic
questions.tip: Always separate P-H (non-ionizable, counts in oxidation state math but not basicity) from P-OH (ionizable, sets the basicity) when analysing phosphorus oxoacids.

questions.text: In the solid state, dinitrogen pentoxide, N2O5, exists as an ionic compound. What is its correct ionic formulation, and what is the hybridization of the cation present?
options: [NO2]+[NO3]-, with the cation being linear and sp hybridized
[NO]+[NO4]-, with the cation being sp2 hybridized
N2O5 remains fully covalent even in the solid state
[NO3]+[NO2]-, with the cation being bent and sp2 hybridized
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the ionic nature of solid N2O5**
In the solid state, N2O5 ionizes into the nitryl (nitronium-like) cation \( NO_{2}^{+}\) and the nitrate anion \( NO_{3}^{-}\), rather than existing as a covalent molecular solid.

**Step 2: Determine the geometry and hybridization of the cation**
The \( NO_{2}^{+}\) cation is isoelectronic with \( CO_{2}\), having 2 N=O bonds and no lone pair on nitrogen, giving it a linear shape and \( sp\) hybridization; the \( NO_{3}^{-}\) anion, by contrast, is trigonal planar and \( sp^{2}\) hybridized.

**Final Answer**
Recognizing this ionic structure explains why solid N2O5 behaves as an ionic crystal (high melting point, conducts when molten) despite the molecule appearing purely covalent on paper.
Final answer: A) [NO2]+[NO3]-, with the cation being linear and sp hybridized
questions.tip: Solid-state N2O5 is a classic example of a p-block oxide that is covalent as a gas-phase molecule but ionic ([NO2]+[NO3]-) in its solid lattice.

questions.text: In ozone, O3, both O-O bond lengths are found to be equal and intermediate between typical O-O single and O=O double bond lengths. What is the reason for this?
options: Ozone is a resonance hybrid of two equivalent structures, and delocalization of the pi electron density makes both O-O bonds identical with a bond order of 1.5
The central oxygen atom is sp3 hybridized with no delocalization
Hydrogen bonding equalizes the bond lengths
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the resonance structures of ozone**
Ozone has a bent structure with a central O atom bonded to two terminal O atoms; it can be drawn as two equivalent resonance structures, each with one O=O double bond and one O-O single bond, differing only in which side carries the double bond.

**Step 2: Connect resonance to equal bond lengths**
The true structure is a resonance hybrid, delocalizing pi electron density equally over both O-O linkages; consequently both bonds are identical, with an intermediate bond order of 1.5 and intermediate bond length (128 pm), rather than one single and one double bond.

**Final Answer**
This resonance-driven bond equalization is the same reasoning used for carbonate, nitrate, and other resonance-stabilized species in inorganic chemistry.
Final answer: A) Ozone is a resonance hybrid of two equivalent structures, and delocalization of the pi electron density makes both O-O bonds identical with a bond order of 1.5
questions.tip: Whenever two experimentally identical bond lengths appear where structures with distinct single/double bonds seem possible, resonance delocalization is almost always the explanation.

questions.text: Oxygen shows a maximum covalency of 4, while sulfur can show covalency up to 6 (as in SF6). What is the main reason for this difference?
options: Oxygen's valence shell (n=2) has no accessible d-orbitals to expand its octet, unlike sulfur (n=3), which has vacant 3d orbitals available for bonding
Oxygen is more electronegative than sulfur
Oxygen has a larger atomic radius than sulfur
Oxygen forms only ionic bonds with other elements
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Compare the valence shells of oxygen and sulfur**
Oxygen is a period-2 element, so its valence shell contains only \( 2s\) and \( 2p\) orbitals (a maximum of 4 orbitals, hence a maximum covalency of 4, e.g. in \( H_{3}O^{+}\) or \( [BeO_{4}]\)-type coordination).

**Step 2: Explain sulfur's higher covalency**
Sulfur is a period-3 element with energetically accessible \( 3d\) orbitals in its valence shell; these can be used (along with 3s and 3p) to accommodate more than 4 bonding pairs, allowing compounds like \( SF_{6}\) where sulfur is hexacoordinate.

**Final Answer**
This is a specific instance of the general period-2-versus-period-3 rule: elements without valence d-orbitals cannot expand their octet beyond 4 bonds.
Final answer: A) Oxygen's valence shell (n=2) has no accessible d-orbitals to expand its octet, unlike sulfur (n=3), which has vacant 3d orbitals available for bonding
questions.tip: Whenever an 'expanded octet' compound like SF6, PCl5, or ClF3 appears, remember it is only possible because the central atom is from period 3 or beyond, with accessible d-orbitals.

questions.text: What is the correct order of acidic strength for the group 16 hydrides H2O, H2S, H2Se, and H2Te?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Identify the factor controlling acidic strength here**
The acidic strength of a hydride (its ability to release H+ in water) depends primarily on the strength of the H-E bond that must be broken; a weaker bond ionizes more readily.

**Step 2: Apply the trend down the group**
As atomic size of the central atom increases down group 16 (O to Te), the H-E bond becomes longer with poorer orbital overlap and hence weaker, even though electronegativity of E decreases. The bond-strength effect dominates, so acidic strength increases down the group: \( H_{2}O < H_{2}S < H_{2}Se < H_{2}Te\).

**Final Answer**
This trend of increasing acidity down a group (opposite to the electronegativity trend) is a common exam trap; bond enthalpy, not electronegativity, dominates for binary hydride acidity trends.
Final answer: A) H2O < H2S < H2Se < H2Te
questions.tip: For binary hydride acidity within a group, always check bond dissociation enthalpy trends first — they usually dominate over electronegativity.

questions.text: What is the hybridization of sulfur in the SO3 molecule (gas-phase monomer)?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Count the electron domains around sulfur**
In SO3, sulfur forms three sigma bonds to three oxygen atoms and has no lone pair remaining on the central atom (the S-O pi bonding uses d-orbital participation on top of the sigma framework).

**Step 2: Assign the hybridization and geometry**
Three electron domains with zero lone pairs corresponds to \( sp^{2}\) hybridization, giving SO3 a trigonal planar molecular geometry with O-S-O bond angles of 120 degrees.

**Final Answer**
This trigonal planar SO3 monomer exists in the gas phase, though the solid readily trimerizes or polymerizes through S-O-S linkages.
Final answer: B) sp2
questions.tip: Count sigma bond pairs plus lone pairs on the central atom to fix hybridization: 3 domains and 0 lone pairs always means sp2 and trigonal planar.

questions.text: The boiling point of H2O (373 K) is much higher than that of H2S (213 K), even though oxygen has a lower molar mass than sulfur. What is the main reason for this anomaly?
options: Extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding between water molecules, arising from oxygen's small size and high electronegativity
The O-H covalent bond is intrinsically much stronger than any intermolecular force in H2S
Water has a higher molecular weight than H2S
H2O is an ionic compound while H2S is covalent
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Identify the intermolecular forces in each hydride**
Oxygen is small and highly electronegative, allowing water molecules to form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds, in which the highly polarized O-H bond of one molecule interacts strongly with a lone pair on the oxygen of a neighbouring molecule, building an extensive 3-dimensional network.

**Step 2: Contrast with H2S**
Sulfur is larger and less electronegative than oxygen, so S-H bonds are far less polar, and H2S can only form weak van der Waals (dispersion) forces between molecules. Much less energy is needed to separate H2S molecules, giving it an anomalously low boiling point despite its higher molar mass.

**Final Answer**
This anomalously high boiling point of water due to hydrogen bonding is why water remains liquid at room temperature while all its heavier group 16 hydride analogues are gases.
Final answer: A) Extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding between water molecules, arising from oxygen's small size and high electronegativity
questions.tip: Hydrogen bonding anomalies (unusually high mp/bp) always occur for hydrides of the smallest, most electronegative elements: F, O, N — remember this trio.

questions.text: What is the average oxidation number of sulfur in sodium tetrathionate, Na2S4O6?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Set up the oxidation number equation for the whole formula**
Let the total (summed) oxidation number contributed by the 4 sulfur atoms be x. Sodium contributes \( +1\) each (2 Na atoms) and oxygen contributes \( -2\) each (6 O atoms), and the compound is neutral: \[ 2(+1) + x + 6(-2) = 0 \]

**Step 2: Solve for the average oxidation state per sulfur atom**
\[ 2 + x - 12 = 0 \Rightarrow x = +10 \] Dividing by the 4 sulfur atoms gives an average oxidation number of \( \frac{+10}{4} = +2.5\) per sulfur atom.

**Final Answer**
This fractional value arises because tetrathionate, S4O6^2-, actually contains two structurally distinct types of sulfur (2 central S-S chain atoms near 0 and 2 terminal -SO3 sulfur atoms near +5); the simple algebraic method only gives their average.
Final answer: A) +2.5
questions.tip: A fractional oxidation number in an algebra-based calculation is a signal that the molecule contains chemically non-equivalent atoms of that element — always sanity-check with the actual structure.

questions.text: SF6 is remarkably inert to hydrolysis by water, even though sulfur is in a high +6 oxidation state that would normally be expected to be readily attacked by nucleophiles. What is the main reason for this kinetic inertness?
options: The octahedral geometry of SF6 sterically and electronically shields the central sulfur atom, leaving no accessible low-energy pathway for a water molecule to attack the sulfur centre
SF6 is completely non-polar and therefore chemically unreactive by definition
The S-F bonds in SF6 are ionic in character
Sulfur lacks d-orbitals needed for hydrolysis to occur
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the structure of SF6**
SF6 is a highly symmetric octahedral molecule ( \( sp^{3}d^{2}\) hybridized sulfur) with 6 equivalent, strong S-F bonds and no lone pair on sulfur.

**Step 2: Explain the kinetic (not thermodynamic) inertness**
Although hydrolysis of SF6 to sulfate and HF would be thermodynamically favourable, the symmetric arrangement of 6 fluorine atoms completely surrounds and shields the sulfur centre, blocking any nucleophilic approach by a water molecule; with no accessible transition state, the reaction essentially does not occur under normal conditions, making SF6 kinetically inert and safe to use as an electrical insulator.

**Final Answer**
This distinction between thermodynamic favourability and kinetic inertness (steric shielding preventing an otherwise favourable reaction) is an important recurring exam concept.
Final answer: A) The octahedral geometry of SF6 sterically and electronically shields the central sulfur atom, leaving no accessible low-energy pathway for a water molecule to attack the sulfur centre
questions.tip: Whenever a compound is described as 'thermodynamically unstable but does not react', suspect kinetic (steric or activation-energy) inertness rather than thermodynamic stability.

questions.text: The F-F bond dissociation enthalpy is unexpectedly lower than the Cl-Cl bond dissociation enthalpy, even though fluorine atoms are smaller than chlorine atoms. What explains this anomaly?
options: Strong repulsion between the closely spaced, non-bonding lone pairs on the two small fluorine atoms weakens the F-F bond
Fluorine has a lower electronegativity than chlorine
The F2 molecule is ionic in character
Fluorine atoms have a larger atomic radius than chlorine atoms
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the small size of fluorine**
Fluorine is the smallest halogen; in F2, the two nuclei (and their 3 non-bonding lone pairs each) are forced very close together because of this small size.

**Step 2: Connect this to bond weakening**
The lone pairs on the two adjacent fluorine atoms experience strong interelectronic (lone pair-lone pair) repulsion, which significantly weakens the F-F sigma bond, overriding the bond-strengthening effect normally expected from good small-atom orbital overlap. As a result, the F-F bond dissociation enthalpy (about 159 kJ/mol) is lower than that of Cl-Cl (about 242 kJ/mol).

**Final Answer**
This lone pair repulsion is also why F2 is one of the most reactive and thermodynamically favourable oxidizers/fluorinating agents despite its high electronegativity.
Final answer: A) Strong repulsion between the closely spaced, non-bonding lone pairs on the two small fluorine atoms weakens the F-F bond
questions.tip: Whenever F2's unusually low bond enthalpy comes up, the cause is always lone pair-lone pair repulsion from its small size, not electronegativity.

questions.text: Among the hydrogen halides, HF is a weak acid in aqueous solution, while HCl, HBr, and HI are all strong acids. What is the main reason for this?
options: The very high H-F bond dissociation enthalpy combined with strong hydrogen bonding (between HF molecules and with water) reduces the availability of free H+ and F- ions
Fluorine is the least electronegative halogen
HF is a purely covalent, non-polar molecule
HF has the largest bond length among the hydrogen halides
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Compare H-X bond strengths**
The H-F bond is by far the strongest bond among the hydrogen halides (about 569 kJ/mol), due to the small size of fluorine allowing excellent orbital overlap with hydrogen; this makes the bond very difficult to break for ionization.

**Step 2: Add the effect of hydrogen bonding**
Additionally, HF molecules engage in extensive hydrogen bonding with each other and with water (forming species such as \( HF_{2}^{-}\)), which further stabilizes undissociated HF and reduces the effective concentration of free \( H^{+}\) ions in solution, so HF ionizes only partially, unlike HCl, HBr, and HI, which have much weaker H-X bonds and dissociate essentially completely.

**Final Answer**
This combination of a very strong H-F bond plus hydrogen bonding is why HF is the outlier weak acid in an otherwise strong-acid series.
Final answer: A) The very high H-F bond dissociation enthalpy combined with strong hydrogen bonding (between HF molecules and with water) reduces the availability of free H+ and F- ions
questions.tip: HF being a weak acid is a classic exception exam question: cite both the exceptionally strong H-F bond and hydrogen bonding, not just one factor.

questions.text: Interhalogen compounds (formed between two different halogens) are generally more reactive than the parent halogens themselves (except F2). What is the reason for this?
options: The X-Y bond in an interhalogen compound is weaker than the X-X bond of the larger halogen involved, because the greater the electronegativity and size difference between X and Y, the more polarized and easily broken the bond becomes
Interhalogen compounds are fully ionic solids
Interhalogen compounds contain no unpaired electrons and are therefore very stable
Interhalogen molecules are always larger than the parent halogen molecules
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall how interhalogens are structured**
An interhalogen compound XYn forms between two halogens of different size and electronegativity, with the larger, less electronegative halogen (X) as the central atom bonded to the smaller, more electronegative halogen (Y).

**Step 2: Explain the resulting bond weakness**
Because X and Y differ in size and electronegativity, the X-Y bond is more polar and generally weaker than the X-X bond found in the halogen X2 (which has two identical, well-matched atoms); this weaker, more easily cleaved bond makes interhalogens undergo bond-breaking reactions more readily, so they are typically more chemically reactive than the pure halogens (F2 itself is an exception because its own X-X bond is anomalously weak due to lone pair repulsion).

**Final Answer**
This enhanced reactivity is why interhalogens like ClF3 and BrF3 are used as powerful fluorinating agents.
Final answer: A) The X-Y bond in an interhalogen compound is weaker than the X-X bond of the larger halogen involved, because the greater the electronegativity and size difference between X and Y, the more polarized and easily broken the bond becomes
questions.tip: Interhalogens are almost always more reactive than the parent halogens because their heteronuclear X-Y bond is weaker and more polar than a homonuclear X-X bond.

questions.text: What is the molecular shape of ClF3, based on VSEPR theory?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Count the electron domains around the central chlorine**
Chlorine in ClF3 has 7 valence electrons; it forms 3 bond pairs with the 3 fluorine atoms and retains 2 lone pairs, giving 5 total electron domains, i.e. \( AX_{3}E_{2}\) with \( sp^{3}d\) hybridization.

**Step 2: Place the lone pairs to minimize repulsion**
Five electron domains adopt a trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry; the two lone pairs preferentially occupy equatorial positions (since equatorial lone pairs experience fewer, weaker 90-degree repulsions than axial ones), leaving the 3 bonded fluorine atoms in a T-shaped molecular arrangement.

**Final Answer**
This is a standard VSEPR result: with an AX3E2 arrangement, the molecular shape is always T-shaped, as also seen in other trihalides of the heavier halogens.
Final answer: B) T-shaped
questions.tip: For AX3E2 species (5 electron domains, 2 lone pairs), always place both lone pairs equatorial to get the characteristic T-shaped molecular geometry.

questions.text: Although the electron gain enthalpy of chlorine is more negative than that of fluorine, F2 is still found to be a stronger oxidizing agent than Cl2 in aqueous solution. What best explains this?
options: F2 has a low bond dissociation enthalpy and F- has a very high (highly negative) hydration enthalpy, and together these more than compensate for fluorine's less negative electron gain enthalpy
Fluorine has a larger atomic radius than chlorine
Cl2 is a completely non-polar, unreactive molecule
F2 has a much higher boiling point than Cl2
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the steps that determine overall oxidizing power in solution**
The overall oxidizing power of a halogen in water depends on the sum of three enthalpy terms: bond dissociation enthalpy of X2 (energy cost to atomize), electron gain enthalpy (energy released on forming X-), and hydration enthalpy of X- (energy released on dissolving X- in water).

**Step 2: Apply the values for F2 versus Cl2**
F2 has an unusually low bond dissociation enthalpy (due to lone pair-lone pair repulsion, easy to atomize) and F- has a very high magnitude hydration enthalpy (because of its very small ionic size); these two favourable terms outweigh fluorine's electron gain enthalpy being slightly less negative than chlorine's, making F2 overall the stronger oxidizing agent in aqueous solution.

**Final Answer**
This shows that oxidizing power cannot be judged from electron gain enthalpy alone; the full thermodynamic cycle (dissociation, electron gain, hydration) must be considered.
Final answer: A) F2 has a low bond dissociation enthalpy and F- has a very high (highly negative) hydration enthalpy, and together these more than compensate for fluorine's less negative electron gain enthalpy
questions.tip: When electron gain enthalpy alone seems to contradict an observed reactivity trend, check bond dissociation enthalpy and hydration enthalpy — together they usually resolve the anomaly.

questions.text: In the interhalogen compound IF7, what are the hybridization of iodine and the resulting molecular geometry?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Count the electron domains around iodine**
Iodine, with 7 valence electrons, forms 7 sigma bonds to 7 fluorine atoms in IF7, using all of its valence electrons for bonding and leaving no lone pairs; this requires 7 hybrid orbitals to accommodate 7 bond pairs.

**Step 2: Assign hybridization and geometry**
Seven orbitals are obtained by mixing \( 5s, 5p^{3}, \text{and } 5d^{3}\) orbitals, giving \( sp^{3}d^{3}\) hybridization; with 7 bond pairs and 0 lone pairs, the geometry that minimizes repulsion is pentagonal bipyramidal (5 fluorine atoms in an equatorial pentagon plus 2 axial fluorine atoms).

**Final Answer**
IF7 has the highest coordination number among common interhalogens, possible only because iodine is large enough to accommodate 7 smaller fluorine atoms around it.
Final answer: A) sp3d3, pentagonal bipyramidal
questions.tip: The maximum coordination number 7 (pentagonal bipyramidal, sp3d3) among interhalogens is uniquely achieved by IF7, since only the large iodine atom can host 7 fluorines.

questions.text: Unlike the other halogens, fluorine does not form oxoacids in which it exhibits a positive oxidation state (there is no analogue of HClO4 for fluorine). What is the correct explanation for this?
options: Fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen, so it cannot show a positive oxidation state when bonded to oxygen, and it also lacks accessible d-orbitals needed to expand its octet and bond to multiple oxygen atoms
Fluorine atoms are too small to bond to oxygen at all
All oxides of fluorine are thermodynamically unstable and decompose instantly
Fluorine has an unusually low ionization enthalpy that prevents oxoacid formation
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall how oxidation states are assigned using electronegativity**
In any bond, the more electronegative atom is assigned the negative oxidation state. Fluorine is the most electronegative element of all, more electronegative even than oxygen, so in any F-O bond, fluorine must be assigned a negative (or zero) oxidation state; it can never be positive versus oxygen, unlike chlorine, bromine, and iodine, which are all less electronegative than oxygen and so can adopt positive oxidation states (+1 to +7) in oxoacids such as \( HClO_{4}\).

**Step 2: Add the structural limitation**
Additionally, fluorine (period 2) has no valence d-orbitals available to expand its octet and bond to several oxygen atoms the way chlorine does in \( ClO_{4}^{-}\); consequently fluorine forms only oxygen difluoride, \( OF_{2}\) (where oxygen, not fluorine, is formally in a positive +2 state), rather than any fluorine oxoacid.

**Final Answer**
This dual reasoning (fluorine's extreme electronegativity plus its lack of d-orbitals) is the standard explanation for why fluorine is anomalous even among its own halogen family regarding oxoacid formation.
Final answer: A) Fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen, so it cannot show a positive oxidation state when bonded to oxygen, and it also lacks accessible d-orbitals needed to expand its octet and bond to multiple oxygen atoms
questions.tip: Fluorine's inability to form oxoacids traces back to it being more electronegative than oxygen itself — it simply cannot take a positive oxidation state versus O.

questions.text: Noble gases exist as monoatomic gases and show very low chemical reactivity. What is the fundamental reason for this?
options: Their atoms already possess a completely filled, highly stable valence electron configuration (ns2np6, or 1s2 for He), which requires very high energy to disturb by adding or removing electrons
They have unusually high atomic mass
They possess strongly negative electron gain enthalpies that make them chemically active
Noble gas atoms are held together by strong metallic bonding
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the electronic configuration of noble gases**
Every noble gas atom has a completely filled valence shell: \( ns^{2}np^{6}\) for Ne through Rn, or \( 1s^{2}\) for helium; this closed-shell arrangement is exceptionally stable.

**Step 2: Connect this to their reactivity**
Because the valence shell is already full, noble gases have very high ionization enthalpies (removing an electron is difficult) and near-zero or positive electron gain enthalpies (adding an electron is not favourable); with no driving force to lose, gain, or share electrons, they exist as chemically inert, monoatomic gases held together only by weak van der Waals forces.

**Final Answer**
This closed-shell stability is the entire basis for the historical classification of group 18 as the 'inert gases', though later chemistry (e.g. XeF2) showed the heavier members are not completely unreactive.
Final answer: A) Their atoms already possess a completely filled, highly stable valence electron configuration (ns2np6, or 1s2 for He), which requires very high energy to disturb by adding or removing electrons
questions.tip: A completely filled valence shell (high IE, unfavourable electron gain enthalpy) is always the root cause of noble gas inertness.

questions.text: The first noble gas compound, Xe+[PtF6]-, was synthesized by Neil Bartlett. What key observation led him to attempt this synthesis?
options: He noted that the first ionization enthalpy of Xe is very close to that of O2, and since PtF6 was already known to oxidize O2 to O2+[PtF6]-, he reasoned PtF6 might similarly oxidize Xe
He observed that Xe reacts spontaneously with all halogens at room temperature
He found that PtF6 itself behaves chemically like a noble gas
He discovered that Xe is naturally a strong reducing agent under all conditions
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the analogy Bartlett drew from O2 chemistry**
Bartlett had earlier observed that PtF6, a very powerful oxidizer, could oxidize molecular oxygen to the dioxygenyl cation, forming the ionic solid \( O_{2}^{+}[PtF_{6}]^{-}\).

**Step 2: Apply this to xenon**
He then noted that the first ionization enthalpy of Xe (about 1170 kJ/mol) is remarkably close to that of \( O_{2}\) (about 1175 kJ/mol); reasoning that if PtF6 was strong enough to remove an electron from O2, it should also be able to remove an electron from Xe, he successfully reacted the two gases to isolate the ionic solid \( Xe^{+}[PtF_{6}]^{-}\) in 1962, the first noble gas compound ever prepared.

**Final Answer**
This discovery overturned the long-held belief that noble gases were completely chemically inert, opening up the entire field of noble gas chemistry.
Final answer: A) He noted that the first ionization enthalpy of Xe is very close to that of O2, and since PtF6 was already known to oxidize O2 to O2+[PtF6]-, he reasoned PtF6 might similarly oxidize Xe
questions.tip: Bartlett's key insight was comparing ionization enthalpies of Xe and O2 — a close match in IE was the clue that a common oxidizer (PtF6) could act on both.

questions.text: What is the molecular shape of XeF4?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Count electron domains around xenon**
Xenon in XeF4 has 8 valence electrons; it forms 4 bond pairs with fluorine atoms and retains 2 lone pairs, giving 6 total electron domains ( \( AX_{4}E_{2}\)), which corresponds to \( sp^{3}d^{2}\) hybridization and an octahedral electron-pair geometry.

**Step 2: Place the lone pairs to minimize repulsion**
To minimize lone pair-lone pair repulsion (the strongest type of repulsion), the two lone pairs occupy mutually trans (opposite, 180 degree) positions in the octahedron; the remaining 4 fluorine atoms then lie in a single plane, giving XeF4 a square planar molecular shape.

**Final Answer**
This square planar shape is a classic VSEPR result for any AX4E2 species, also seen in other main-group tetrafluorides with two lone pairs.
Final answer: B) Square planar
questions.tip: For AX4E2 species (6 electron domains, 2 lone pairs), placing the lone pairs trans to each other always gives a square planar molecular shape.

questions.text: What is the molecular shape of XeOF4?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Count the electron domains around xenon**
In XeOF4, xenon is bonded to 4 fluorine atoms and 1 oxygen atom (via a Xe=O bond, counted as one electron domain) and retains 1 lone pair, giving 6 total electron domains ( \( AX_{5}E\)), corresponding to \( sp^{3}d^{2}\) hybridization with an octahedral electron-pair geometry.

**Step 2: Determine the molecular shape after placing the lone pair**
With 5 bonded atoms (4 F + 1 O) and 1 lone pair occupying one vertex of the octahedron, the resulting molecular shape (all atoms pushed slightly away from the lone pair) is square pyramidal, with the oxygen typically at the apex.

**Final Answer**
This AX5E arrangement giving a square pyramidal shape is directly analogous to other 5-bond-plus-1-lone-pair species predicted by VSEPR theory.
Final answer: B) Square pyramidal
questions.tip: For AX5E species (6 electron domains, 1 lone pair), the molecular shape is always square pyramidal.

questions.text: Among the noble gases, only the heavier members, particularly xenon (and to a lesser extent krypton and radon), readily form chemical compounds. What is the main reason for this?
options: Their ionization enthalpy is relatively low (due to large atomic size and greater electron shielding), which allows their outer electrons to be removed by strong oxidizers/highly electronegative elements like F and O to form bonds
Heavier noble gases have a strongly negative electron gain enthalpy
Heavier noble gases are radioactive, which makes them chemically reactive
Heavier noble gases have an odd number of valence electrons
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the trend in ionization enthalpy down group 18**
Ionization enthalpy decreases down group 18 as atomic size increases and additional inner shells shield the valence electrons more effectively from the nucleus; helium through argon have very high ionization enthalpies, essentially too high for any reagent to overcome.

**Step 2: Connect this to compound formation**
Xenon's ionization enthalpy is low enough to be overcome by extremely strong oxidizers such as F2 (under suitable conditions) or PtF6, allowing formation of Xe-F and Xe-O bonds (e.g. XeF2, XeF4, XeF6, XeO3); krypton's higher ionization enthalpy allows only limited chemistry (e.g. KrF2), and radon, despite a favourable low ionization enthalpy, is difficult to study due to its intense radioactivity.

**Final Answer**
This trend explains why noble gas chemistry is essentially confined to xenon, with only minor extensions to krypton and radon.
Final answer: A) Their ionization enthalpy is relatively low (due to large atomic size and greater electron shielding), which allows their outer electrons to be removed by strong oxidizers/highly electronegative elements like F and O to form bonds
questions.tip: Only the heaviest, lowest-ionization-enthalpy noble gases (Xe primarily) form real compounds — always with the most electronegative elements, F and O.

questions.text: Complete hydrolysis of XeF6 with water produces which of the following as the xenon-containing product?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the stepwise hydrolysis of XeF6**
XeF6 undergoes partial hydrolysis in stages: reaction with limited water first gives XeOF4, further hydrolysis gives XeO2F2, and each successive replacement of a fluorine atom by an oxygen-containing group requires additional water.

**Step 2: Determine the product of complete hydrolysis**
With excess water, all 6 fluorine atoms are eventually replaced, giving the balanced overall reaction: \[ XeF_{6} + 3H_{2}O \rightarrow XeO_{3} + 6HF \] The product XeO3 is a colourless, pyramidal ( \( sp^{3}\) hybridized, one lone pair), and dangerously explosive solid.

**Final Answer**
Recognizing this stepwise fluorine-to-oxygen substitution pattern (XeF6 to XeOF4 to XeO2F2 to XeO3) is key to predicting xenon oxide/oxyfluoride products from hydrolysis questions.
Final answer: A) XeO3 (plus HF)
questions.tip: Complete hydrolysis of XeF6 always ends at XeO3 plus 6 HF; partial hydrolysis stops at the intermediate oxyfluorides XeOF4 or XeO2F2.

questions.text: Xenon reacts directly with fluorine gas under different conditions to give XeF2, XeF4, or XeF6, depending on the relative proportion of F2 used and the reaction conditions. Which statement correctly relates the amount of F2 used to the fluoride product formed?
options: A greater relative excess of F2 (generally together with higher temperature and/or pressure) favours formation of higher fluorides such as XeF6, while a lower, closer-to-stoichiometric proportion of F2 favours XeF2
A greater excess of F2 always favours XeF2 over the higher fluorides
The Xe to F2 ratio has no influence on which fluoride is formed
XeF6 forms preferentially only when F2 is the limiting reagent
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the general reaction and its stepwise nature**
Xenon fluorides form by successive substitution of F atoms onto the Xe centre: \( Xe \rightarrow XeF_{2} \rightarrow XeF_{4} \rightarrow XeF_{6}\); each additional substitution requires more available fluorine to proceed further.

**Step 2: Apply Le Chatelier-type reasoning to the F2 proportion**
A close-to-1:1 or modestly excess Xe:F2 ratio under milder conditions favours stopping at the first substitution product, XeF2; progressively larger excesses of F2, generally combined with higher temperature and/or pressure to drive the equilibrium further, are needed to push the reaction on to XeF4 and then to the fully substituted XeF6.

**Final Answer**
This dependence on F2 excess and reaction severity is the standard basis on which the three binary xenon fluorides are selectively synthesized in the laboratory.
Final answer: A) A greater relative excess of F2 (generally together with higher temperature and/or pressure) favours formation of higher fluorides such as XeF6, while a lower, closer-to-stoichiometric proportion of F2 favours XeF2
questions.tip: More F2 (and harsher conditions) always pushes xenon fluoride synthesis toward the higher fluorides (XeF4, XeF6); less F2 under milder conditions stops at XeF2.

questions.text: Among the chlorine oxoacids HClO4, HClO3, HClO2, and HClO, which is the strongest acid?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the rule governing oxoacid strength for a common central atom**
For oxoacids of the same central atom, acidic strength increases with the number of highly electronegative oxo (Cl=O) groups attached to that atom, because more oxo groups withdraw electron density more strongly through the central atom, weakening the O-H bond and stabilizing the resulting conjugate base by delocalizing the negative charge over more oxygens.

**Step 2: Apply this to the four chlorine oxoacids**
The number of oxo groups (and hence the oxidation state of Cl) increases in the order \( HClO < HClO_{2} < HClO_{3} < HClO_{4}\) (Cl oxidation states +1, +3, +5, +7); HClO4, with 3 oxo groups on chlorine, therefore has the strongest electron-withdrawing effect and is the strongest acid.

**Final Answer**
This rule (more oxo groups means stronger acid) is one of the most frequently tested facts about oxoacid strength trends in p-block chemistry.
Final answer: A) HClO4
questions.tip: For oxoacids of the same central atom, acid strength always increases with the number of =O (oxo) groups: HClO4 > HClO3 > HClO2 > HClO.

questions.text: The basicity of a phosphorus oxoacid (the number of replaceable/ionizable hydrogen atoms) is determined by:
options: The total number of hydrogen atoms present in the molecular formula
The number of P-OH (ionizable hydroxyl) groups only
The number of P=O bonds present
The total number of oxygen atoms present
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Distinguish the two types of hydrogen in phosphorus oxoacids**
Phosphorus oxoacids can contain hydrogen bonded either to oxygen (P-O-H) or directly to phosphorus (P-H). Only hydrogen bonded through oxygen can be released as H+ in water; P-H bonds are non-polar, essentially covalent, and do not ionize.

**Step 2: Apply this rule to determine basicity**
Therefore basicity equals only the count of P-OH groups, not the total hydrogen count: \( H_{3}PO_{2}\) has 1 P-OH (plus 2 P-H) so it is monobasic; \( H_{3}PO_{3}\) has 2 P-OH (plus 1 P-H) so it is dibasic; \( H_{3}PO_{4}\) has 3 P-OH (and no P-H) so it is tribasic.

**Final Answer**
This distinction between ionizable P-OH hydrogens and non-ionizable P-H hydrogens is essential for correctly predicting the basicity of any phosphorus oxoacid.
Final answer: B) The number of P-OH (ionizable hydroxyl) groups only
questions.tip: Never assume basicity equals the total H count in a formula; always identify which hydrogens are bonded to oxygen (ionizable) versus directly to the central atom (non-ionizable).

questions.text: Sulfuric acid, H2SO4, is a dibasic acid. What structural feature makes it dibasic?
options: It contains exactly 2 ionizable S-OH groups
It contains 4 oxygen atoms in total
It has 2 hydrogen atoms bonded directly to sulfur
It contains 1 S=O bond and 3 S-OH groups
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the structure of sulfuric acid**
H2SO4 has a tetrahedral sulfur centre bonded to 2 oxygen atoms via S=O double bonds and to 2 hydroxyl groups via S-OH single bonds; there are no S-H bonds.

**Step 2: Connect structure to basicity**
Since only the hydrogens attached through oxygen (the 2 S-OH groups) can ionize as H+ in water, H2SO4 releases exactly 2 replaceable protons, making it a dibasic (diprotic) acid, consistent with its formation of both normal sulfate (SO4^2-) and acid sulfate (HSO4-) salts.

**Final Answer**
Recognizing the S=O versus S-OH split in the structure is the key to correctly predicting basicity for any sulfur oxoacid.
Final answer: A) It contains exactly 2 ionizable S-OH groups
questions.tip: Basicity of a sulfur (or phosphorus, chlorine) oxoacid always equals the number of -OH groups on the central atom, never the total oxygen or hydrogen count.

questions.text: What is the oxidation state of chlorine in chloric acid, HClO3?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Set up the oxidation number equation**
Let the oxidation number of chlorine be x. In the neutral molecule HClO3, hydrogen is +1 and each of the 3 oxygen atoms is -2: \[ (+1) + x + 3(-2) = 0 \]

**Step 2: Solve for x**
\[ 1 + x - 6 = 0 \Rightarrow x = +5 \] So chlorine is in the +5 oxidation state in HClO3.

**Final Answer**
This +5 oxidation state fits the pattern where HClO, HClO2, HClO3, and HClO4 correspond to Cl oxidation states +1, +3, +5, and +7 respectively, each increasing by 2 as an additional oxo group is added.
Final answer: C) +5
questions.tip: Memorize the oxidation state pattern for chlorine oxoacids: HClO(+1), HClO2(+3), HClO3(+5), HClO4(+7) — each step adds one oxygen and 2 units of oxidation state.

questions.text: Both HNO3 and H3PO4 have their central atom in the +5 oxidation state, yet HNO3 is a much stronger acid than H3PO4. What best explains this difference?
options: HNO3 has fewer -OH groups (just 1) and a small, highly electronegative nitrogen forming strong N=O bonds, so the resulting NO3- conjugate base is efficiently stabilized by delocalization over fewer oxygens; H3PO4 has 3 -OH groups, which dilutes the electron-withdrawing effect and gives a weaker acid
Nitrogen is less electronegative than phosphorus
H3PO4 is completely unstable in aqueous solution
HNO3 simply has more hydrogen atoms than H3PO4
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Compare the structures of the two acids**
HNO3 has 1 N-OH group and 2 N=O bonds (using strong \( p\pi-p\pi\) bonding, since N is a small period-2 atom); H3PO4 has 3 P-OH groups and only 1 P=O bond, since phosphorus (period 3) is larger and less able to form strong pi bonds with oxygen.

**Step 2: Connect the structural difference to acid strength**
With only 1 OH group and strong electron withdrawal from the small, electronegative N through its 2 oxo groups, the O-H bond in HNO3 is weakened substantially and the conjugate base NO3- is well stabilized by resonance, so HNO3 ionizes essentially completely (strong acid). In H3PO4, the electron-withdrawing effect from just 1 oxo group is spread thin, and having 3 OH groups means each dissociation is less favoured, so H3PO4 ionizes only partially (weak/moderate acid).

**Final Answer**
This comparison shows that acid strength depends not just on the oxidation state of the central atom, but critically on the number of oxo groups relative to hydroxyl groups.
Final answer: A) HNO3 has fewer -OH groups (just 1) and a small, highly electronegative nitrogen forming strong N=O bonds, so the resulting NO3- conjugate base is efficiently stabilized by delocalization over fewer oxygens; H3PO4 has 3 -OH groups, which dilutes the electron-withdrawing effect and gives a weaker acid
questions.tip: Do not assume oxoacids with the same central-atom oxidation state have similar acid strength — always compare the actual number of =O versus -OH groups.

questions.text: Pyrophosphoric acid, H4P2O7, is formed by condensation of two orthophosphoric acid units with loss of one water molecule. What is its basicity?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the structure of pyrophosphoric acid**
H4P2O7 consists of two PO4 tetrahedra joined together by sharing one bridging oxygen atom (a P-O-P linkage); each phosphorus atom retains 2 terminal P-OH groups and 1 terminal P=O group.

**Step 2: Count the total ionizable groups**
Since only P-OH groups are ionizable, and each of the 2 phosphorus atoms contributes 2 such groups, the total number of ionizable hydrogens is \( 2 \times 2 = 4\), making H4P2O7 tetrabasic.

**Final Answer**
This structural approach (count ionizable P-OH groups per P atom, then sum over all P atoms) works for any condensed phosphorus oxoacid, including tripolyphosphoric acid and beyond.
Final answer: C) 4
questions.tip: For condensed (bridged) oxoacids, always count P-OH groups per central atom individually, then add across all central atoms present.

questions.text: Sulfurous acid, H2SO3, in which sulfur is in the +4 oxidation state, can act as both an oxidizing agent and a reducing agent depending on the reaction partner. What explains this dual behaviour?
options: +4 is an intermediate oxidation state of sulfur, lying between its highest common state (+6) and lower states (such as 0 or -2), so sulfur in H2SO3 can either be oxidized further (acting as a reducing agent) or reduced (acting as an oxidizing agent)
H2SO3 is thermally unstable and decomposes before it can react
Sulfur has no d-orbitals available in H2SO3
H2SO3 is a very strong acid, which automatically makes it a strong oxidizing agent
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the range of oxidation states accessible to sulfur**
Sulfur commonly exhibits oxidation states ranging from -2 (as in sulfides, H2S) up to +6 (as in sulfates, H2SO4); +4, as found in H2SO3/sulfite, lies exactly between these extremes.

**Step 2: Explain the resulting dual redox behaviour**
Because +4 is intermediate, sulfur in H2SO3 can lose electrons and be oxidized to +6 when reacting with a stronger oxidizer (H2SO3 then behaves as a reducing agent, e.g. reducing acidified KMnO4), or it can gain electrons and be reduced to a lower state (0 or -2) when reacting with a stronger reducing agent (H2SO3 then behaves as an oxidizing agent, e.g. oxidizing H2S to elemental sulfur).

**Final Answer**
This principle, that species in an intermediate oxidation state can show dual redox character, applies broadly across p-block oxoacid and oxoanion chemistry (e.g. also seen for nitrogen in HNO2).
Final answer: A) +4 is an intermediate oxidation state of sulfur, lying between its highest common state (+6) and lower states (such as 0 or -2), so sulfur in H2SO3 can either be oxidized further (acting as a reducing agent) or reduced (acting as an oxidizing agent)
questions.tip: Whenever a central atom is in an intermediate oxidation state (neither its lowest nor highest), expect the compound to be capable of acting as both an oxidizing and a reducing agent.

questions.text: Orthophosphorous acid, H3PO3, on heating undergoes disproportionation to give orthophosphoric acid (H3PO4) and phosphine (PH3), according to 4H3PO3 to 3H3PO4 + PH3. Why is this classified as a disproportionation reaction?
options: Phosphorus, starting from a single oxidation state (+3) in H3PO3, is simultaneously oxidized to +5 (in H3PO4) and reduced to -3 (in PH3) within the same reaction, i.e. the same element in one oxidation state acts as both the oxidizing and the reducing agent
H3PO3 is simply unstable and breaks down without any change in oxidation state
Phosphorus only changes its physical state during the reaction, not its oxidation state
The reaction is a straightforward acid-base neutralization with no redox character
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the definition of disproportionation**
A disproportionation reaction is a redox reaction in which an element present in a single, intermediate oxidation state in the reactant is converted into two (or more) different oxidation states of that same element among the products, meaning it is simultaneously oxidized and reduced.

**Step 2: Verify this pattern for the phosphorus reaction**
In \( 4H_{3}PO_{3} \rightarrow 3H_{3}PO_{4} + PH_{3}\), phosphorus starts uniformly at +3 oxidation state in H3PO3; in the products, 3 out of every 4 phosphorus atoms are oxidized up to +5 (in H3PO4), while the remaining 1 out of 4 is reduced down to -3 (in PH3), exactly fitting the disproportionation pattern.

**Final Answer**
Recognizing this pattern (one starting oxidation state splitting into a higher and a lower state among products) is essential for correctly classifying and balancing similar oxoacid disproportionation reactions.
Final answer: A) Phosphorus, starting from a single oxidation state (+3) in H3PO3, is simultaneously oxidized to +5 (in H3PO4) and reduced to -3 (in PH3) within the same reaction, i.e. the same element in one oxidation state acts as both the oxidizing and the reducing agent
questions.tip: To identify a disproportionation reaction, always track the oxidation state of one specific element across all reactants and products — if it splits into both a higher and a lower value, it is disproportionation.
