Heating the sodium salt of a carboxylic acid with soda lime removes the carboxylate group as \( CO_3^{2-} \), replacing it with a hydrogen atom; \( CaO \) in soda lime simply prevents the caustic \( NaOH \) from corroding the glass container.
\[ CH_3COONa + NaOH \rightarrow CH_4 + Na_2CO_3 \]

**Step 2: Track the carbon count**
Acetate (\( CH_3COO^- \)) has two carbons; decarboxylation removes the carboxyl carbon (as carbonate), leaving only the methyl carbon behind as methane.

**Step 3: Eliminate the other options**
Ethane, ethylene, and acetylene all require two carbons in the product, but decarboxylation of a two-carbon acid necessarily leaves only one carbon.

**Final Answer**
Decarboxylation of sodium acetate with soda lime is the classic laboratory method for preparing methane.
Final answer: B) Methane
questions.tip: Decarboxylation with soda lime always removes exactly one carbon (the -COOH carbon) from the acid, shortening the chain by one.

questions.text: In the free-radical chlorination of methane, which step below is a propagation step that both consumes and regenerates a radical, keeping the chain reaction going?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Distinguish the three mechanistic stages**
A radical chain mechanism has an initiation step (creates radicals from a stable molecule), propagation steps (a radical reacts with a stable molecule to give a new radical, keeping radical count constant), and termination steps (two radicals combine and destroy each other).

**Step 2: Classify each option**
\( Cl_2 \rightarrow 2Cl^{\bullet} \) is initiation (homolysis under light/heat, radical count increases from 0 to 2); \( Cl^{\bullet}+Cl^{\bullet}\rightarrow Cl_2 \) and \( CH_3^{\bullet}+CH_3^{\bullet}\rightarrow C_2H_6 \) are termination steps (two radicals combine to give a closed-shell molecule).

**Step 3: Identify the correct propagation step**
In \( CH_4+Cl^{\bullet}\rightarrow CH_3^{\bullet}+HCl \), one radical (\( Cl^{\bullet} \)) is consumed while a new radical (\( CH_3^{\bullet} \)) is produced, so the total radical count stays at one throughout - this is the hallmark of a propagation step.

**Final Answer**
Propagation steps sustain the chain by converting one radical into another without net loss of radicals.
Final answer: B) \( CH_4 + Cl^{\bullet} \rightarrow CH_3^{\bullet} + HCl \)
questions.tip: Count radicals on each side of an elementary step: same count on both sides means propagation; 2 to 0 or 0 to 2 means termination or initiation.

questions.text: Free-radical monobromination of 2-methylbutane occurs with high selectivity for one particular hydrogen. Which monobromo product forms as the major product, and why?
options: 1-bromo-2-methylbutane, because primary C-H bonds are most abundant
2-bromo-3-methylbutane, because secondary radicals are most stable
2-bromo-2-methylbutane, because it proceeds through the most stable tertiary free radical
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall why bromination is highly selective**
Unlike chlorination, bromination has a late, highly endothermic hydrogen-abstraction step, so the transition state closely resembles the resulting free radical (Hammond postulate); consequently the stability of the intermediate radical almost entirely controls which product dominates.

**Step 2: Locate the different types of hydrogens in 2-methylbutane**
\[ CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-CH_3 \]
This molecule has primary hydrogens (on \( C1 \) and the methyl branch), one tertiary hydrogen (on \( C2 \)), and secondary hydrogens (on \( C3 \)).

**Step 3: Apply radical stability order**
Radical stability follows tertiary > secondary > primary (due to greater hyperconjugation and inductive electron release from more alkyl groups), so abstraction of the single tertiary hydrogen at \( C2 \) is heavily favoured despite there being only one such hydrogen.

**Final Answer**
The bromine radical selectively abstracts the tertiary hydrogen, giving 2-bromo-2-methylbutane as the overwhelmingly major product.
Final answer: C) 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, because it proceeds through the most stable tertiary free radical
questions.tip: For bromination, always predict the major product via the most stable (usually tertiary) radical, not the statistically most abundant hydrogen type.

questions.text: How many structurally distinct monochloro products (constitutional isomers) are formed on free-radical monochlorination of 2-methylpropane (isobutane)?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Draw the structure and identify distinct hydrogen environments**
\[ (CH_3)_3CH \]
Isobutane has nine equivalent primary hydrogens (on the three identical methyl groups) and one tertiary hydrogen (on the central carbon) - only two chemically distinct types of hydrogen exist by symmetry.

**Step 2: Replace each distinct hydrogen type by chlorine**
Substitution at any of the nine equivalent primary hydrogens gives the same constitutional isomer, 1-chloro-2-methylpropane; substitution at the single tertiary hydrogen gives 2-chloro-2-methylpropane.

**Step 3: Count distinct constitutional products**
Even though there are ten hydrogens in total, they fall into only two symmetry-distinct sets, so only two different structural isomers of the monochloride can form (though not in equal amounts, since tertiary substitution is favoured per hydrogen).

**Final Answer**
Counting isomers requires counting distinct hydrogen environments by symmetry, not the total number of hydrogens.
Final answer: B) 2
questions.tip: To count structural isomers from monosubstitution, first identify symmetry-equivalent hydrogens - equivalent hydrogens always give the identical product.

questions.text: Which method is preferred over the Wurtz reaction for the efficient synthesis of an unsymmetrical alkane such as 2-methylpentane from two different alkyl fragments?
options: Kolbe electrolysis of a single carboxylic acid
Corey-House synthesis using a lithium dialkylcuprate (Gilman reagent) with an alkyl halide
Catalytic hydrogenation of the corresponding alkene
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the drawback of the Wurtz reaction**
Using two different alkyl halides in a Wurtz reaction gives an inseparable statistical mixture of three coupling products, which makes it unsuitable for cleanly preparing an unsymmetrical alkane.

**Step 2: Recall the Corey-House method**
An alkyl halide is first converted to a lithium dialkylcuprate, \( R_2CuLi \) (a Gilman reagent), by reaction with lithium metal and then cuprous iodide; this cuprate then couples cleanly and selectively with a second, different alkyl halide.
\[ R_2CuLi + R'X \rightarrow R-R' + RCu + LiX \]

**Step 3: Explain why this route is clean**
Because the cuprate reagent reacts specifically with the second halide in a controlled organometallic coupling (rather than via free radicals reacting indiscriminately), only the desired unsymmetrical product forms, without the statistical scrambling seen in Wurtz coupling.

**Final Answer**
Corey-House synthesis is the method of choice whenever an unsymmetrical alkane must be built cleanly from two different alkyl groups.
Final answer: B) Corey-House synthesis using a lithium dialkylcuprate (Gilman reagent) with an alkyl halide
questions.tip: Whenever a synthesis question asks for an unsymmetrical alkane, think Corey-House (Gilman reagent), not Wurtz.

questions.text: What are the products of complete combustion of an alkane in excess oxygen?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the nature of complete combustion**
Complete combustion occurs when a hydrocarbon burns in an adequate (excess) supply of oxygen, fully oxidising every carbon atom to its highest common oxidation state and every hydrogen atom to water.
\[ C_nH_{2n+2} + \frac{3n+1}{2}O_2 \rightarrow nCO_2 + (n+1)H_2O \]

**Step 2: Contrast with limited oxygen supply**
When oxygen is insufficient (incomplete combustion), carbon monoxide or even elemental carbon (soot) forms instead of carbon dioxide; this is a separate, undesired scenario, not complete combustion.

**Step 3: Eliminate the other options**
Options naming carbon monoxide, soot, or hydrogen gas as products describe incomplete combustion or are not thermodynamically favoured products under excess oxygen.

**Final Answer**
Under excess oxygen, every alkane burns completely and exothermically to carbon dioxide and water, which is the basis of alkanes being used as fuels.
Final answer: B) Carbon dioxide and water
questions.tip: Balance combustion equations quickly by first balancing carbon, then hydrogen, then oxygen last.

questions.text: What is the general molecular formula of an open-chain alkene containing one carbon-carbon double bond?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Compare to the saturated alkane formula**
An alkane with \( n \) carbons has \( 2n+2 \) hydrogens; introducing one carbon-carbon double bond removes two hydrogens (one degree of unsaturation) because two fewer sigma C-H bonds are needed once a pi bond forms between two carbons.

**Step 2: Derive the alkene formula**
\[ C_nH_{2n+2} - H_2 = C_nH_{2n} \]

**Step 3: Eliminate the other options**
\( C_nH_{2n+2} \) is saturated (no unsaturation) and \( C_nH_{2n-2} \) corresponds to two degrees of unsaturation (an alkyne, diene, or a ring plus a double bond), neither of which matches a single alkene double bond.

**Final Answer**
One degree of unsaturation (one double bond or one ring) always corresponds to the formula \( C_nH_{2n} \).
Final answer: B) \( C_nH_{2n} \)
questions.tip: Each degree of unsaturation (ring or pi bond) removes exactly 2 hydrogens from the saturated formula \( C_nH_{2n+2} \).

questions.text: According to Markovnikov's rule, when \( HBr \) (in the absence of peroxide) adds to propene, the hydrogen atom attaches predominantly to which carbon?
options: The carbon bearing fewer hydrogen atoms (\( C2 \))
The carbon of the double bond that already bears more hydrogen atoms (\( C1 \))
The carbon farthest from the double bond
questions.answer:
**Step 1: State Markovnikov's rule**
In the ionic (electrophilic) addition of an unsymmetrical reagent \( HX \) to an unsymmetrical alkene, the electrophile (\( H^+ \)) adds so as to generate the more stable carbocation intermediate.

**Step 2: Apply to propene**
\[ CH_3-CH=CH_2 + H^{+} \rightarrow CH_3-\overset{+}{C}H-CH_3 \ (\text{secondary, favoured}) \]
Protonation at the terminal (\( C1 \), already bearing two H atoms) carbon places the positive charge on \( C2 \), giving a more stable secondary carbocation, compared to protonation at \( C2 \) which would give a less stable primary carbocation.

**Step 3: Complete the addition**
The bromide ion then attacks the secondary carbocation at \( C2 \), giving 2-bromopropane as the major product.

**Final Answer**
Hydrogen adds to the carbon already richer in hydrogen, so that the more stable (here, secondary) carbocation forms as the intermediate - this is the essence of Markovnikov addition.
Final answer: B) The carbon of the double bond that already bears more hydrogen atoms (\( C1 \))
questions.tip: Remember Markovnikov as 'the rich get richer': H adds to the carbon that already has more H atoms.

questions.text: Dehydrohalogenation of 2-bromobutane with alcoholic \( KOH \) gives a mixture of but-1-ene and but-2-ene. According to Saytzeff's (Zaitsev's) rule, which alkene is the major product?
options: But-2-ene, the more substituted (more stable) alkene
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall Saytzeff's rule**
In a beta-elimination (dehydrohalogenation) reaction, when more than one alkene can form, the more highly substituted (and therefore thermodynamically more stable) alkene is the major product, because the transition state leading to it is lower in energy.

**Step 2: Identify the possible products from 2-bromobutane**
\[ CH_3-CHBr-CH_2-CH_3 \]
Loss of \( HBr \) can remove a beta-hydrogen from \( C1 \) (giving but-1-ene, a monosubstituted alkene) or from \( C3 \) (giving but-2-ene, a disubstituted, more stable alkene).

**Step 3: Apply the stability argument**
But-2-ene has two alkyl groups on the double-bond carbons (disubstituted), giving greater hyperconjugative and inductive stabilisation than the monosubstituted but-1-ene, so it forms preferentially.

**Final Answer**
Saytzeff's rule predicts that elimination reactions favour the more substituted, more stable alkene as the major product.
Final answer: B) But-2-ene, the more substituted (more stable) alkene
questions.tip: For elimination questions, always count alkyl substituents on the double bond - more substituents means more stable and more favoured by Saytzeff's rule.

questions.text: The peroxide (Kharasch) effect, giving anti-Markovnikov addition of \( HBr \) to alkenes, is observed only with \( HBr \) and not with \( HCl \) or \( HI \). What is the main reason for this?
options: HCl and HI do not dissolve in the reaction medium
Both the initiation and propagation steps are exothermic only for HBr; for HCl the addition of the halogen radical is endothermic and for HI the hydrogen-abstraction step is endothermic
Peroxides only decompose in the presence of bromine atoms
HCl and HI cannot form free radicals under any conditions
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the radical chain mechanism of the peroxide effect**
Peroxides generate radicals that abstract a hydrogen from \( HX \) to form an \( X^{\bullet} \) radical, which then adds to the terminal carbon of the alkene to generate the more stable secondary/tertiary radical; a second \( HX \) molecule then donates \( H^{\bullet} \) to complete the chain.

**Step 2: Evaluate the energetics for each halogen acid**
For \( HCl \), the addition of a chlorine radical to the alkene is endothermic (the \( C-Cl \) bond formed is not strong enough to compensate for breaking the pi bond), so the chain does not propagate efficiently; for \( HI \), the iodine radical adds exothermically, but the subsequent hydrogen-abstraction step from \( HI \) is endothermic because the \( H-I \) bond is weak and iodine radicals tend to simply recombine.

**Step 3: Contrast with HBr**
For \( HBr \), both the bromine-radical addition step and the hydrogen-abstraction step are exothermic, so the full radical chain proceeds efficiently only in this case.

**Final Answer**
Only with \( HBr \) are both propagation steps of the radical chain energetically favourable, which is why the peroxide effect is unique to \( HBr \) among the hydrogen halides.
Final answer: B) Both the initiation and propagation steps are exothermic only for HBr; for HCl the addition of the halogen radical is endothermic and for HI the hydrogen-abstraction step is endothermic
questions.tip: Remember: the peroxide (Kharasch) effect applies ONLY to HBr among HX acids - HCl and HI always add via the normal Markovnikov ionic pathway.

questions.text: Ozonolysis of 2-methylbut-2-ene, \( (CH_3)_2C=CH-CH_3 \), followed by reductive work-up with \( Zn/H_2O \), gives which pair of carbonyl products?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the ozonolysis reaction**
Ozonolysis cleaves the carbon-carbon double bond completely, and each doubly bonded carbon becomes a carbonyl carbon; reductive work-up (\( Zn/H_2O \), or dimethyl sulfide) prevents further oxidation, so aldehydes are obtained (not carboxylic acids) if a hydrogen was present on that carbon.

**Step 2: Identify each half of the alkene**
\[ (CH_3)_2C=CH-CH_3 \]
One alkene carbon bears two methyl groups (no hydrogen on it), and the other bears one hydrogen and one methyl group.

**Step 3: Assign the products**
The disubstituted carbon (no H) becomes a ketone, \( (CH_3)_2C=O \) (acetone/propan-2-one); the monosubstituted carbon (one H) becomes an aldehyde, \( CH_3CHO \) (acetaldehyde/ethanal).

**Final Answer**
Ozonolysis cleaves the double bond into two carbonyl fragments whose substitution pattern mirrors that of the original alkene carbons - a fully substituted carbon gives a ketone, a carbon with one H gives an aldehyde.
Final answer: B) Acetone and acetaldehyde
questions.tip: In ozonolysis, mentally split the double bond in half and put an oxygen on each carbon - count the remaining substituents to decide ketone versus aldehyde.

questions.text: Hydroboration-oxidation of propene (\( BH_3 \) followed by \( H_2O_2/OH^- \)) gives which major alcohol product?
options: Propan-1-ol, via anti-Markovnikov, syn addition with boron on the less hindered carbon
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the regiochemistry of hydroboration**
Boron in \( BH_3 \) is electron-deficient and sterically bulky; it adds to the less substituted (less hindered) carbon of the double bond, while a partial negative charge develops on the more substituted carbon, giving anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry overall.

**Step 2: Apply to propene**
\[ CH_3-CH=CH_2 + BH_3 \rightarrow CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-BH_2 \ (\text{boron on terminal carbon}) \]

**Step 3: Perform the oxidation step**
Treatment with alkaline hydrogen peroxide replaces the \( C-B \) bond with a \( C-OH \) bond with retention of configuration (syn addition overall, no carbocation rearrangement), placing the \( OH \) group on the terminal carbon.

**Final Answer**
Hydroboration-oxidation is the standard method for achieving clean anti-Markovnikov, syn hydration of an alkene, giving propan-1-ol from propene.
Final answer: B) Propan-1-ol, via anti-Markovnikov, syn addition with boron on the less hindered carbon
questions.tip: Hydroboration-oxidation is the go-to method whenever a question needs the anti-Markovnikov alcohol without carbocation rearrangement.

questions.text: Dehydration of butan-2-ol with concentrated \( H_2SO_4 \) predominantly gives which alkene?
options: But-2-ene, following Zaitsev's rule for the more substituted, more stable alkene
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the mechanism of acid-catalysed dehydration**
Protonation of the hydroxyl group by \( H_2SO_4 \) creates a good leaving group (water), which departs to form a carbocation at \( C2 \); loss of a beta-hydrogen (E1 mechanism) then generates the alkene.

**Step 2: Identify possible beta-hydrogens**
\[ CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_2-CH_3 \]
A beta-hydrogen can be removed from \( C1 \) (giving but-1-ene) or from \( C3 \) (giving but-2-ene).

**Step 3: Apply Zaitsev's rule**
But-2-ene is disubstituted (more alkyl groups on the double bond) and hence more stable than the monosubstituted but-1-ene, so the more substituted alkene forms as the major product, exactly as in dehydrohalogenation.

**Final Answer**
Acid-catalysed dehydration of alcohols, like dehydrohalogenation, is governed by Zaitsev's rule and favours the more substituted alkene.
Final answer: B) But-2-ene, following Zaitsev's rule for the more substituted, more stable alkene
questions.tip: Both dehydration of alcohols and dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides follow the same Zaitsev preference for the more substituted alkene.

questions.text: An alkene undergoes ozonolysis (followed by reductive work-up) to give only one product, acetone (propan-2-one), with no other carbonyl compound detected. What must the structure of the starting alkene be?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Interpret 'only one product' from ozonolysis**
Ozonolysis normally cleaves a double bond into two separate carbonyl fragments; obtaining only a single product means the alkene must be symmetrical, so that both halves of the cleaved double bond are identical.

**Step 2: Work backward from acetone**
Since the sole product is acetone, \( (CH_3)_2C=O \), each carbon of the original double bond must have carried two methyl groups (no hydrogen), because ozonolysis simply replaces the double bond carbon's remaining substituents with a \( C=O \).

**Step 3: Reconstruct the alkene**
Joining two \( (CH_3)_2C= \) fragments back together across the double bond gives \( (CH_3)_2C=C(CH_3)_2 \), i.e. 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene, a fully tetrasubstituted, symmetrical alkene.

**Final Answer**
A single ozonolysis product always signals a symmetrically substituted alkene; here that alkene is 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene.
Final answer: C) 2,3-Dimethylbut-2-ene, a symmetrical tetrasubstituted alkene
questions.tip: In reverse-ozonolysis problems, a single carbonyl product always means the parent alkene was symmetrical about the double bond.

questions.text: In the peroxide-catalysed (anti-Markovnikov) addition of \( HBr \) to 2-methylpropene (isobutylene), the bromine radical adds preferentially to which carbon, and why?
options: The more substituted carbon, because it is more electronegative
The terminal (\( =CH_2 \)) carbon, because this generates the more stable tertiary free radical at the other carbon
Either carbon randomly, since radicals show no preference
The terminal carbon, because bromine radicals are too large to reach the substituted carbon
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the mechanism of radical addition**
In the peroxide-initiated chain mechanism, a bromine radical (generated from \( HBr \) by a peroxide-derived radical) adds first to one carbon of the double bond, and the resulting unpaired electron resides on the other carbon as a new radical intermediate.

**Step 2: Compare the two possible radical intermediates**
\[ (CH_3)_2C=CH_2 + Br^{\bullet} \rightarrow (CH_3)_2\overset{\bullet}{C}-CH_2Br \ (\text{tertiary radical, favoured}) \]
Addition of \( Br^{\bullet} \) to the terminal \( CH_2 \) carbon leaves the unpaired electron on the more substituted carbon, forming a tertiary radical, which is far more stable (through hyperconjugation and inductive donation from three methyl groups) than the primary radical that would form from addition at the substituted carbon.

**Step 3: Complete the chain**
This stable tertiary radical then abstracts a hydrogen atom from another \( HBr \) molecule, giving the anti-Markovnikov product 1-bromo-2-methylpropane and regenerating a bromine radical to continue the chain.

**Final Answer**
Radical addition, just like ionic addition, is controlled by the stability of the intermediate formed - here, bromine adds to the terminal carbon so that the more stable tertiary radical results.
Final answer: B) The terminal (\( =CH_2 \)) carbon, because this generates the more stable tertiary free radical at the other carbon
questions.tip: For peroxide-effect problems, always draw both possible radical intermediates and pick the pathway giving the more substituted (more stable) radical.

questions.text: Arrange ethene, propene, and 2-methylpropene in increasing order of rate of electrophilic addition with \( HCl \).
options: All three react at the same rate
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Identify the rate-determining step**
Electrophilic addition to an alkene proceeds through protonation of the double bond to form a carbocation intermediate, and the rate of this slow step depends directly on how stable that carbocation is.

**Step 2: Compare the carbocations formed**
Protonation of ethene gives a primary carbocation (\( CH_3CH_2^+ \)); protonation of propene gives a secondary carbocation (\( CH_3\overset{+}{C}HCH_3 \)); protonation of 2-methylpropene gives a tertiary carbocation (\( (CH_3)_3C^+ \)).

**Step 3: Apply carbocation stability order**
Since tertiary carbocations are more stable than secondary, which are more stable than primary (due to increasing hyperconjugation and +I donation from alkyl groups), the alkene giving the more stable carbocation reacts faster.

**Final Answer**
Greater alkyl substitution on the double bond stabilises the transition state leading to the carbocation, so reactivity increases from ethene to propene to 2-methylpropene.
Final answer: B) Ethene < propene < 2-methylpropene
questions.tip: More substituted alkenes are both more stable AND more reactive toward electrophilic addition - stability of the alkene and of the resulting carbocation move together.

questions.text: What is the general molecular formula of an open-chain hydrocarbon containing one carbon-carbon triple bond?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Count degrees of unsaturation in a triple bond**
A carbon-carbon triple bond consists of one sigma bond and two pi bonds, which corresponds to two degrees of unsaturation (equivalent to two double bonds or one double bond plus one ring).

**Step 2: Subtract hydrogens from the saturated formula**
Each degree of unsaturation removes two hydrogens from the fully saturated alkane formula \( C_nH_{2n+2} \).
\[ C_nH_{2n+2} - 2H_2 = C_nH_{2n-2} \]

**Step 3: Eliminate the other options**
\( C_nH_{2n} \) matches only one degree of unsaturation (an alkene), and \( C_nH_{2n-4} \) would correspond to three degrees of unsaturation, more than a single triple bond provides.

**Final Answer**
A single triple bond always corresponds to the formula \( C_nH_{2n-2} \), reflecting its two degrees of unsaturation.
Final answer: C) \( C_nH_{2n-2} \)
questions.tip: A triple bond equals 2 degrees of unsaturation, meaning 4 fewer hydrogens than the saturated alkane formula.

questions.text: Ethyne (acetylene) gas is passed into ammoniacal silver nitrate solution. What is observed, and why does this reaction occur?
options: No visible change, since alkynes are unreactive to metal salts
A white precipitate of silver acetylide forms, because the terminal (sp C-H) hydrogen of ethyne is acidic enough to be displaced by \( Ag^+ \)
A red precipitate of silver oxide forms due to reduction
A black precipitate of metallic silver forms due to oxidation of the alkyne
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the acidity of terminal alkynes**
The hydrogen attached to an \( sp \)-hybridised carbon in a terminal alkyne is unusually acidic (compared to alkanes/alkenes) because the \( sp \) orbital holding the C-H bonding electrons has 50 percent s-character, holding the bonding electrons closer to the carbon nucleus and stabilising the resulting carbanion (acetylide ion).

**Step 2: Apply this acidity to the reaction with \( Ag^+ \)**
\[ HC \equiv CH + 2[Ag(NH_3)_2]^{+} \rightarrow AgC \equiv CAg\downarrow + 2NH_4^{+} + 2NH_3 \]
The acidic terminal hydrogens are readily displaced by the silver ion from the ammoniacal complex, forming an insoluble silver acetylide salt.

**Step 3: Note the diagnostic value**
This reaction is used as a chemical test to distinguish terminal alkynes (which have this acidic C-H) from alkenes and internal alkynes (which do not react this way).

**Final Answer**
The white precipitate of silver acetylide confirms the presence of an acidic terminal alkyne C-H bond.
Final answer: B) A white precipitate of silver acetylide forms, because the terminal (sp C-H) hydrogen of ethyne is acidic enough to be displaced by \( Ag^+ \)
questions.tip: Ammoniacal AgNO3 (or Cu2Cl2) precipitate formation is the standard test for a terminal alkyne's acidic C-H, not for the triple bond itself.

questions.text: 1,2-Dibromoethane is treated with excess alcoholic \( KOH \). What is the final organic product, and what type of reaction produces it?
options: Ethyne, via double dehydrohalogenation (two successive eliminations of HBr)
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall that vicinal dihalides give alkynes on double elimination**
A vicinal dihalide (halogens on adjacent carbons) can undergo two successive dehydrohalogenation (E2) reactions with a strong base like alcoholic \( KOH \); the first elimination gives a vinyl halide, and the second elimination removes the remaining halogen and an adjacent hydrogen.

**Step 2: Track the two eliminations**
\[ BrCH_2-CH_2Br \rightarrow CH_2=CHBr \rightarrow HC \equiv CH \]
The first step (alcoholic KOH) removes one \( HBr \) to form bromoethene (vinyl bromide); the second step removes the remaining \( HBr \) to introduce the second pi bond, giving the triple bond.

**Step 3: Confirm the final product**
With excess base and sufficient heating, elimination proceeds all the way to completion, converting the vicinal dihalide fully into the terminal alkyne.

**Final Answer**
Double dehydrohalogenation of a vicinal dihalide with excess alcoholic KOH is a standard laboratory route to alkynes, here giving ethyne.
Final answer: B) Ethyne, via double dehydrohalogenation (two successive eliminations of HBr)
questions.tip: Vicinal or geminal dihalides both give alkynes with excess alcoholic KOH - two eliminations are needed to install the triple bond.

questions.text: Propyne reacts with 2 mol of \( HBr \). What is the major final product, and what governs its regiochemistry?
options: 2,2-Dibromopropane, via Markovnikov addition in both addition steps
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall that alkynes undergo two successive Markovnikov additions**
In the absence of peroxides, each addition of \( HX \) to a triple bond follows Markovnikov's rule, with the electrophile (\( H^+ \)) adding so as to generate the more stabilised cationic intermediate.

**Step 2: Perform the first addition**
\[ CH_3-C\equiv CH + HBr \rightarrow CH_3-CBr=CH_2 \]
Protonation occurs at the terminal carbon (giving the more stable secondary vinyl cation), placing bromine on \( C2 \).

**Step 3: Perform the second addition**
\[ CH_3-CBr=CH_2 + HBr \rightarrow CH_3-CBr_2-CH_3 \]
The second \( HBr \) again adds by Markovnikov's rule; since \( C2 \) already bears a bromine (the more substituted, more stabilised position via the adjacent alkyl and halogen groups), the second bromine also ends up on \( C2 \), giving a geminal dibromide.

**Final Answer**
Successive Markovnikov additions of \( HBr \) to propyne place both bromine atoms on the same (more substituted) carbon, giving 2,2-dibromopropane.
Final answer: B) 2,2-Dibromopropane, via Markovnikov addition in both addition steps
questions.tip: Double addition of HX to a terminal alkyne (no peroxide) gives a geminal dihalide, with both halogens on the internal carbon.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly ranks the acidity of the C-H bond in ethane, ethene, and ethyne?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Identify the factor controlling C-H acidity here**
The acidity of a C-H bond attached to a carbon of a given hybridisation depends on the percentage of s-character in that carbon's hybrid orbital - more s-character means the bonding (and lone pair, in the conjugate base) electrons are held closer to the nucleus, stabilising the carbanion formed on deprotonation.

**Step 2: Compare s-character across hybridisations**
Ethyne's carbon is \( sp \) hybridised (50 percent s-character), ethene's is \( sp^2 \) hybridised (33 percent s-character), and ethane's is \( sp^3 \) hybridised (25 percent s-character).

**Step 3: Rank the acidity accordingly**
Greater s-character correlates directly with greater acidity of the attached C-H bond, since the resulting carbanion is more stabilised.

**Final Answer**
Acidity increases with increasing s-character of the carbon hybrid orbital, giving the order ethyne > ethene > ethane.
Final answer: B) Ethyne > ethene > ethane
questions.tip: Remember the s-character trend: sp (50%) > sp2 (33%) > sp3 (25%), and higher s-character always means a more acidic attached C-H.

questions.text: Propyne is treated with dilute \( H_2SO_4 \) in the presence of \( HgSO_4 \) (acid-catalysed hydration). What is the major organic product?
options: Propan-2-one (acetone), via Markovnikov addition of water followed by keto-enol tautomerisation
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the mechanism of mercury-catalysed hydration**
\( Hg^{2+} \) coordinates to the triple bond and activates it toward nucleophilic attack by water, which adds according to Markovnikov's rule, placing \( OH \) on the more substituted carbon of the triple bond.

**Step 2: Form the enol intermediate**
\[ CH_3-C\equiv CH + H_2O \rightarrow CH_3-C(OH)=CH_2 \ (\text{enol}) \]

**Step 3: Tautomerise to the stable keto form**
The enol is unstable relative to its keto tautomer and rapidly rearranges via proton transfer to the more stable carbonyl compound.
\[ CH_3-C(OH)=CH_2 \rightarrow CH_3-CO-CH_3 \]

**Final Answer**
Markovnikov hydration of a terminal alkyne (other than ethyne itself) gives a methyl ketone after keto-enol tautomerisation; here propyne gives acetone.
Final answer: C) Propan-2-one (acetone), via Markovnikov addition of water followed by keto-enol tautomerisation
questions.tip: Only ethyne gives an aldehyde (acetaldehyde) on hydration; every other terminal alkyne gives a methyl ketone via the enol intermediate.

questions.text: But-1-yne and but-2-yne are treated separately with ammoniacal \( AgNO_3 \) solution. Explain the difference in observation.
options: Both give a white precipitate, since all alkynes react identically
Neither reacts, since alkynes never react with silver salts
But-1-yne gives a white precipitate (terminal C-H is acidic); but-2-yne shows no reaction (no acidic terminal hydrogen, being an internal alkyne)
But-2-yne gives a precipitate while but-1-yne does not, because internal triple bonds are more reactive
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Draw both structures and locate the triple bond**
\[ \text{But-1-yne: } CH_3CH_2-C\equiv CH \qquad \text{But-2-yne: } CH_3-C\equiv C-CH_3 \]
But-1-yne is a terminal alkyne (triple bond at the end of the chain, with one hydrogen directly on an \( sp \) carbon); but-2-yne is an internal alkyne (triple bond in the middle, with alkyl groups, not hydrogen, on both \( sp \) carbons).

**Step 2: Recall the requirement for the silver acetylide test**
Only a hydrogen directly bonded to an \( sp \)-hybridised carbon is acidic enough to be displaced by \( Ag^+ \) from the ammoniacal complex.

**Step 3: Apply this to each compound**
But-1-yne possesses this acidic \( \equiv C-H \) and therefore reacts to give a white precipitate of the silver acetylide; but-2-yne has no hydrogen on either \( sp \) carbon (both bear methyl groups) and so cannot form a precipitate.

**Final Answer**
The ammoniacal \( AgNO_3 \) test distinguishes terminal from internal alkynes precisely because only the terminal alkyne has an acidic \( sp \) C-H bond available for displacement.
Final answer: C) But-1-yne gives a white precipitate (terminal C-H is acidic); but-2-yne shows no reaction (no acidic terminal hydrogen, being an internal alkyne)
questions.tip: Before predicting a positive silver acetylide test, always check whether the triple bond is terminal (has a bare sp C-H) or internal.

questions.text: 2-Butyne is reduced separately using (i) Lindlar's catalyst (\( Pd/CaCO_3 \) poisoned with quinoline) and (ii) sodium metal in liquid ammonia. What are the respective stereochemical outcomes?
options: Lindlar's catalyst gives cis-2-butene (syn addition of H2); Na/liquid NH3 gives trans-2-butene (anti addition via a radical-anion mechanism)
Lindlar's catalyst gives trans-2-butene; Na/liquid NH3 gives cis-2-butene
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the mechanism of Lindlar hydrogenation**
Lindlar's catalyst is a poisoned (partially deactivated) palladium catalyst that adsorbs the alkyne and hydrogen onto its metal surface, delivering both hydrogen atoms to the same face of the triple bond (syn addition), and it is deliberately poisoned to stop reduction at the alkene stage rather than continuing to the alkane.

**Step 2: Determine the geometry from syn addition**
Syn addition of two hydrogens to an internal alkyne places the two methyl groups on the same side of the resulting double bond, giving the cis (Z) alkene.
\[ CH_3-C\equiv C-CH_3 \xrightarrow{H_2,\ Lindlar} cis\text{-}CH_3CH=CHCH_3 \]

**Step 3: Contrast with dissolving-metal reduction**
Sodium in liquid ammonia reduces the alkyne through a radical-anion mechanism in which the two hydrogens are delivered from opposite faces at different mechanistic steps (anti addition), placing the methyl groups on opposite sides and giving the trans (E) alkene.
\[ CH_3-C\equiv C-CH_3 \xrightarrow{Na,\ liq.\ NH_3} trans\text{-}CH_3CH=CHCH_3 \]

**Final Answer**
The choice of reducing agent for an internal alkyne dictates alkene stereochemistry: Lindlar's catalyst (syn addition) gives the cis-alkene, while Na/liquid ammonia (anti addition) gives the trans-alkene.
Final answer: C) Lindlar's catalyst gives cis-2-butene (syn addition of H2); Na/liquid NH3 gives trans-2-butene (anti addition via a radical-anion mechanism)
questions.tip: Pair 'Lindlar equals cis' and 'Na/liquid NH3 equals trans' as a fixed fact for alkyne-to-alkene stereoselective reduction questions.

questions.text: According to Huckel's rule, a planar, cyclic, fully conjugated ring system is aromatic if the number of pi electrons in the ring equals:
options: \( 4n \), where \( n \) is any whole number
Any even number of pi electrons
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the origin of Huckel's rule**
Huckel's rule comes from molecular orbital theory: in a planar, fully conjugated monocyclic system, the pi molecular orbitals arrange into one lowest-energy orbital and successive degenerate pairs; complete extra stabilisation (aromaticity) results only when all bonding orbitals are completely filled with no electrons in non-bonding or antibonding orbitals.

**Step 2: Translate this into an electron-counting formula**
This complete filling of bonding orbitals happens precisely when the total pi-electron count is \( 4n+2 \) (giving values 2, 6, 10, 14, ... for \( n=0,1,2,3,... \)).

**Step 3: Eliminate the other options**
\( 4n \) pi electrons (e.g. 4, 8) instead leaves partially filled, degenerate non-bonding/antibonding orbitals, causing antiaromatic destabilisation, not aromaticity; 'exactly 6' is only the specific case for benzene (\( n=1 \)), not the general rule.

**Final Answer**
Huckel's \( 4n+2 \) rule is the general criterion for aromaticity in planar, cyclic, fully conjugated systems, of which benzene (6 pi electrons, \( n=1 \)) is the archetypal example.
Final answer: B) \( 4n+2 \), where \( n = 0, 1, 2, 3, ... \)
questions.tip: Memorise the allowed aromatic pi-electron counts directly: 2, 6, 10, 14 - and remember 4n (4, 8, 12) instead signals antiaromaticity.

questions.text: All six carbon-carbon bonds in benzene have an identical length of about 139 pm, intermediate between a C-C single bond (154 pm) and a C=C double bond (134 pm). What is the best explanation for this?
options: Benzene rapidly interconverts between two Kekule structures, averaging the bond lengths over time
Benzene is a resonance hybrid with its pi electrons delocalised equally over all six carbons, so no single Kekule structure with alternating bonds accurately represents it
Benzene has only single bonds and no double bonds at all
Benzene's bond lengths are simply an experimental error
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the limitation of a single Kekule structure**
A single Kekule structure with three alternating double and single bonds would predict two distinct bond lengths (short double bonds, long single bonds) around the ring, which experimental X-ray data does not show.

**Step 2: Introduce the resonance (delocalisation) description**
Benzene is more accurately described as a single resonance hybrid of two (or more) contributing Kekule structures, in which the six pi electrons are delocalised over all six \( p \) orbitals of the ring simultaneously, rather than genuinely oscillating between two discrete structures.

**Step 3: Connect delocalisation to bond length**
Because the pi-electron density is spread evenly over all six carbon-carbon bonds, each bond acquires intermediate, and identical, partial double-bond character, giving the single observed bond length of about 139 pm.

**Final Answer**
The uniform bond length in benzene is direct experimental evidence for genuine electron delocalisation (resonance), not a rapidly interconverting mixture of two separate molecules.
Final answer: B) Benzene is a resonance hybrid with its pi electrons delocalised equally over all six carbons, so no single Kekule structure with alternating bonds accurately represents it
questions.tip: Never describe benzene as 'oscillating' between Kekule structures in an exam answer - the correct description is a single delocalised resonance hybrid.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a structural requirement for a compound to be classified as aromatic?
options: The ring must be planar (or nearly so)
Every ring atom must be part of a continuous system of overlapping p orbitals (complete conjugation)
The ring must contain an odd number of pi electrons
questions.answer:
**Step 1: List the genuine requirements for aromaticity**
A compound is aromatic if it is (i) cyclic, (ii) planar, so that all p orbitals can align in parallel for maximum overlap, (iii) every atom in the ring has a p orbital available (fully conjugated), and (iv) the ring contains \( 4n+2 \) pi electrons (Huckel's rule).

**Step 2: Test the given option against this list**
'An odd number of pi electrons' is not equivalent to \( 4n+2 \); for example, 4 pi electrons is even but not aromatic (antiaromatic, as in cyclobutadiene), while the precise rule requires specifically 2, 6, 10, 14 electrons, not merely 'any odd number'.

**Step 3: Confirm the other three are correct requirements**
Cyclic, planar, and fully conjugated are indeed all necessary (though not sufficient) conditions; the additional sufficient condition is specifically \( 4n+2 \) pi electrons, not merely 'odd'.

**Final Answer**
'Odd number of pi electrons' is not a valid aromaticity criterion - the precise electron-count rule is \( 4n+2 \), not simply any odd number.
Final answer: D) The ring must contain an odd number of pi electrons
questions.tip: Do not confuse 'odd number of pi electrons' with Huckel's precise 4n+2 rule - always check for the actual count 2, 6, 10, 14, and so on.

questions.text: Benzene typically undergoes electrophilic substitution reactions rather than the addition reactions typical of simple alkenes. What is the main reason for this preference?
options: Benzene has no pi electrons available for addition
Addition would destroy the ring's aromatic delocalisation (resonance stabilisation), whereas substitution regenerates the aromatic ring after the electrophile is incorporated
Benzene's carbon atoms are too far apart for addition to occur
Substitution reactions do not require an electrophile
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Compare the energetics of addition versus substitution**
If an electrophile added across one of benzene's carbon-carbon bonds the way it adds to an alkene, the extensive pi-electron delocalisation (aromatic stabilisation) that lowers benzene's energy would be permanently lost, making the addition product energetically very costly to form.

**Step 2: Describe what happens in substitution instead**
In electrophilic aromatic substitution, the electrophile first adds to give a non-aromatic, resonance-stabilised arenium cation, but then a proton is lost from that same carbon, restoring full conjugation and regenerating the aromatic ring.

**Step 3: Conclude the thermodynamic driving force**
Because substitution allows the ring to recover its aromatic stabilisation while addition would sacrifice it permanently, substitution is strongly favoured energetically over addition for benzene and its derivatives.

**Final Answer**
Aromatic stabilisation is preserved only if the ring's conjugation is restored after reaction, which is exactly what happens in substitution but not in addition.
Final answer: B) Addition would destroy the ring's aromatic delocalisation (resonance stabilisation), whereas substitution regenerates the aromatic ring after the electrophile is incorporated
questions.tip: Whenever asked why benzene resists addition, the key phrase to include is 'aromatic stabilisation/resonance energy is retained only in substitution'.

questions.text: In the nitration of benzene using a mixture of concentrated \( HNO_3 \) and concentrated \( H_2SO_4 \), what electrophilic species does \( H_2SO_4 \) help generate, and what is its role?
options: Hydroxide ion, which acts as a nucleophile
Nitronium ion, \( NO_2^+ \), generated by protonation of nitric acid followed by loss of water; it is the actual electrophile that attacks the ring
Sulfonic acid, which substitutes directly onto the ring
Nitrite ion, \( NO_2^- \), which acts as a base
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the role of sulfuric acid as a stronger acid**
Concentrated \( H_2SO_4 \) protonates nitric acid at its hydroxyl oxygen, since \( H_2SO_4 \) is the stronger acid in this mixture.
\[ HNO_3 + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow H_2NO_3^{+} + HSO_4^{-} \]

**Step 2: Generate the active electrophile**
The protonated nitric acid then loses a molecule of water to form the nitronium ion, a strong electrophile with a full positive charge centred on nitrogen.
\[ H_2NO_3^{+} \rightarrow NO_2^{+} + H_2O \]

**Step 3: Confirm its role in the mechanism**
This nitronium ion, \( NO_2^+ \), is the actual electrophile that attacks the electron-rich benzene ring, forming the resonance-stabilised arenium ion intermediate, which then loses a proton to restore aromaticity and give nitrobenzene.

**Final Answer**
Sulfuric acid's essential role in nitration is generating the potent electrophile \( NO_2^+ \) from nitric acid.
Final answer: B) Nitronium ion, \( NO_2^+ \), generated by protonation of nitric acid followed by loss of water; it is the actual electrophile that attacks the ring
questions.tip: Whenever nitration mechanism is asked, always name the electrophile explicitly as the nitronium ion, NO2+, not simply 'nitric acid'.

questions.text: Direct Friedel-Crafts alkylation of benzene to prepare pure n-propylbenzene is unreliable because the intermediate primary propyl carbocation rearranges to a more stable secondary carbocation. What is the standard alternative route to obtain n-propylbenzene cleanly?
options: Direct chlorination of benzene followed by reduction
Friedel-Crafts acylation with propanoyl chloride/\( AlCl_3 \) to give propiophenone, followed by Clemmensen reduction (Zn-Hg/HCl) to fully reduce the carbonyl to a methylene group
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Diagnose the problem with direct alkylation**
Friedel-Crafts alkylation with 1-chloropropane and \( AlCl_3 \) generates a primary propyl carbocation, which readily undergoes a hydride shift to the more stable secondary isopropyl carbocation, so the major product is actually isopropylbenzene (cumene), not n-propylbenzene.

**Step 2: Recall why acylation avoids this problem**
Friedel-Crafts acylation instead generates an acylium ion (\( R-C\equiv O^+ \)), which is stabilised by resonance delocalisation of the positive charge onto oxygen and therefore does not rearrange, giving a clean, unrearranged aryl ketone.
\[ C_6H_6 + CH_3CH_2COCl \rightarrow C_6H_5-CO-CH_2CH_3 \ (\text{propiophenone}) \]

**Step 3: Reduce the carbonyl to complete the synthesis**
Clemmensen reduction (zinc amalgam and hydrochloric acid) fully reduces the ketone carbonyl to a \( CH_2 \) group without disturbing the aromatic ring, converting propiophenone cleanly into n-propylbenzene.

**Final Answer**
Whenever a straight-chain alkylbenzene is needed, the acylation-then-reduction sequence avoids the rearrangement problem inherent to direct Friedel-Crafts alkylation.
Final answer: B) Friedel-Crafts acylation with propanoyl chloride/\( AlCl_3 \) to give propiophenone, followed by Clemmensen reduction (Zn-Hg/HCl) to fully reduce the carbonyl to a methylene group
questions.tip: Whenever a straight-chain (unbranched) alkylbenzene is the target, default to Friedel-Crafts acylation plus Clemmensen (or Wolff-Kishner) reduction, never direct alkylation.

questions.text: In electrophilic aromatic substitution, what is the name given to the resonance-stabilised, non-aromatic cationic intermediate formed immediately after the electrophile attacks the benzene ring (before loss of a proton)?
options: Arenium ion (sigma complex, also called the benzenonium ion)
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Track the bonding change on electrophile attack**
When an electrophile bonds to one ring carbon, that carbon becomes \( sp^3 \) hybridised, breaking the continuous conjugation and removing that carbon from the delocalised pi system, leaving a positive charge delocalised only over the remaining five conjugated carbons.

**Step 2: Name this intermediate**
This cationic, non-aromatic (but still resonance-stabilised by three contributing structures) intermediate is called the arenium ion, sigma complex, or benzenonium ion.

**Step 3: Distinguish it from the other named species**
Benzyne is a completely different, highly strained triple-bond-containing intermediate formed in nucleophilic aromatic substitution under very strong base conditions, not relevant here; benzyl cation and phenonium ion refer to different cationic species outside the ring or in neighbouring-group participation, not the arenium ion of standard electrophilic substitution.

**Final Answer**
The key intermediate of every electrophilic aromatic substitution is the arenium ion (sigma complex), which then loses a proton to restore aromaticity.
Final answer: B) Arenium ion (sigma complex, also called the benzenonium ion)
questions.tip: Always draw the three resonance structures of the arenium ion intermediate when explaining an EAS mechanism - it demonstrates why substitution restores aromaticity.

questions.text: Toluene is subjected to vigorous oxidation with hot, alkaline potassium permanganate followed by acidification. What is the product?
options: Benzoic acid, since the ring resists oxidation but any benzylic side chain is oxidised all the way to -COOH regardless of its original length
Benzene, since the methyl group is simply removed
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the resistance of the aromatic ring to oxidation**
The aromatic ring itself, being stabilised by delocalisation, is not attacked by strong oxidising agents like hot alkaline \( KMnO_4 \) under these conditions; only a side chain attached to the ring can be oxidised.

**Step 2: Recall the fate of alkyl side chains**
Any alkyl group on the ring that has at least one benzylic hydrogen is oxidised completely down to a single carboxylic acid group directly attached to the ring, regardless of how long the original chain was - all the extra carbons are lost as \( CO_2 \) or other small fragments.

**Step 3: Apply to toluene**
Toluene's single methyl substituent is oxidised at the benzylic position all the way through to \( -COOH \), attached directly to the ring.
\[ C_6H_5-CH_3 \rightarrow C_6H_5-COOH \]

**Final Answer**
Vigorous oxidation of any alkylbenzene with a benzylic hydrogen always converts the side chain into a single -COOH group directly on the ring, here giving benzoic acid from toluene.
Final answer: B) Benzoic acid, since the ring resists oxidation but any benzylic side chain is oxidised all the way to -COOH regardless of its original length
questions.tip: Remember: KMnO4 oxidation of any alkylbenzene side chain (as long as a benzylic H is present) always gives -COOH directly on the ring, no matter the chain length.

questions.text: Which of the following species is aromatic according to Huckel's rule?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Count the pi electrons in each species**
Cyclopentadienyl cation has 4 pi electrons; cyclopentadienyl anion has 6 pi electrons (the extra lone pair from the carbanion occupies a p orbital, joining the ring's conjugation); cycloheptatrienyl anion has 8 pi electrons; cyclobutadiene has 4 pi electrons.

**Step 2: Apply Huckel's 4n+2 rule to each**
Only 6 pi electrons satisfies \( 4n+2 \) (with \( n=1 \)) among these four counts; 4 and 8 pi electrons instead satisfy \( 4n \) (with \( n=1,2 \)), which corresponds to antiaromaticity if the ring is planar and cyclic.

**Step 3: Confirm planarity and cyclic conjugation**
Each of these species, being a fully conjugated monocyclic carbanion/carbocation with every ring atom \( sp^2 \) hybridised and bearing a p orbital, satisfies the structural requirements, so the electron count alone determines aromaticity here.

**Final Answer**
Only the cyclopentadienyl anion has the required \( 4n+2 = 6 \) pi electrons, making it the aromatic species among the four listed.
Final answer: B) Cyclopentadienyl anion (6 pi electrons)
questions.tip: Huckel's rule applies equally to charged ring systems (cations, anions), not just neutral hydrocarbons like benzene - always count total pi electrons including any extra lone pair or missing electron.

questions.text: The hypothetical heat of hydrogenation of 'cyclohexatriene' (three isolated, non-interacting double bonds) can be estimated as three times cyclohexene's heat of hydrogenation, about \( 3 \times (-120) = -360\ kJ/mol \). The experimentally measured heat of hydrogenation of real benzene is about \( -208\ kJ/mol \). What is benzene's approximate resonance (delocalisation) energy?
options: \( 152\ kJ/mol \), the difference between the hypothetical and the actual (lower magnitude) heat of hydrogenation
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Set up the comparison**
Resonance (delocalisation) energy is defined as the extra stability of the real, delocalised molecule compared to a hypothetical reference structure with the same connectivity but localised, non-interacting double bonds; it is measured as the difference between the hypothetical and the actual heat of hydrogenation.

**Step 2: Compute the hypothetical value**
If benzene behaved as three independent, non-conjugated double bonds, hydrogenating it would release three times cyclohexene's heat of hydrogenation.
\[ 3 \times (-120\ kJ/mol) = -360\ kJ/mol \]

**Step 3: Compare to the experimental value and take the difference**
The real benzene releases far less energy on hydrogenation (\( -208\ kJ/mol \)) than the hypothetical structure would, because benzene starts out already unusually stable (lower in energy) due to delocalisation; the resonance energy is the magnitude of this difference.
\[ |-360| - |-208| = 152\ kJ/mol \]

**Final Answer**
Benzene releases about 152 kJ/mol less heat than expected on hydrogenation, and this 'missing' energy is its resonance (delocalisation) energy, a direct experimental measure of aromatic stabilisation.
Final answer: C) \( 152\ kJ/mol \), the difference between the hypothetical and the actual (lower magnitude) heat of hydrogenation
questions.tip: Resonance energy is always (hypothetical heat of hydrogenation) minus (actual, smaller-magnitude, heat of hydrogenation) - the real molecule always releases less heat because it started out more stable.

questions.text: Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation reactions both fail when attempted on nitrobenzene or on aniline. Explain the reason for failure in each case.
options: Both fail simply because AlCl3 is insoluble in both compounds

Nitrobenzene's ring is too strongly deactivated by the electron-withdrawing -NO2 group to be attacked by the electrophile/AlCl3 complex; aniline's basic -NH2 group forms a salt-like complex with the Lewis acid AlCl3, which then acts as a strongly deactivating group on the ring
Both fail because nitrogen atoms poison the AlCl3 catalyst permanently in all cases
Nitrobenzene and aniline are both non-aromatic, so Friedel-Crafts cannot occur
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Analyse the nitrobenzene case**
The strongly electron-withdrawing \( -NO_2 \) group (by both resonance and induction) removes electron density from the ring so severely that the ring is no longer nucleophilic enough to attack the electrophile or the electrophile-\( AlCl_3 \) complex, so no reaction occurs (nitrobenzene is even used as an inert solvent for other Friedel-Crafts reactions for this very reason).

**Step 2: Analyse the aniline case**
The nitrogen lone pair on \( -NH_2 \) is a Lewis base, and it immediately reacts with the Lewis acid catalyst \( AlCl_3 \) to form a salt-like complex, \( C_6H_5-\overset{+}{N}H_2-AlCl_3^{-} \).

**Step 3: Explain the consequence for aniline**
Once complexed, the nitrogen lone pair can no longer donate into the ring by resonance; worse, this complexed nitrogen now behaves as a strongly electron-withdrawing group (similar to a protonated amine), strongly deactivating the ring toward any electrophilic attack.

**Final Answer**
Nitrobenzene fails because its ring is already too deactivated to begin with; aniline fails because its own activating group is neutralised (converted into a deactivating group) by the very Lewis acid catalyst required for the reaction.
Final answer: B) Nitrobenzene's ring is too strongly deactivated by the electron-withdrawing -NO2 group to be attacked by the electrophile/AlCl3 complex; aniline's basic -NH2 group forms a salt-like complex with the Lewis acid AlCl3, which then acts as a strongly deactivating group on the ring
questions.tip: Aniline and strongly deactivated rings (nitrobenzene) are the two classic named exceptions where Friedel-Crafts reactions fail - know the distinct reason for each.

questions.text: How many sigma bonds and how many (delocalised) pi bonds are present in one molecule of benzene, \( C_6H_6 \)?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Count the sigma bonds**
Benzene has six carbon-carbon ring bonds, each of which is a sigma bond, plus six carbon-hydrogen bonds, each also a sigma bond.
\[ 6\ (C-C\ \sigma) + 6\ (C-H\ \sigma) = 12\ \sigma\ \text{bonds} \]

**Step 2: Count the pi electrons and convert to pi bonds**
Each ring carbon contributes one electron in a p orbital perpendicular to the ring plane, giving six pi electrons total; these occupy three completely bonding, delocalised molecular orbitals spanning the whole ring.

**Step 3: Express this as an equivalent number of pi bonds**
Six delocalised pi electrons correspond to three pi bonds' worth of electron density (2 electrons per pi bond), even though this pi density is spread over all six carbons rather than localised into three fixed double bonds.

**Final Answer**
Benzene contains 12 sigma bonds (6 C-C plus 6 C-H) and an equivalent of 3 pi bonds, delocalised as a single system over all six ring carbons.
Final answer: B) 12 sigma bonds and 3 pi bonds
questions.tip: Count sigma bonds by simply counting all directly connected atom pairs; count pi bonds by dividing the total pi electrons by two, regardless of whether they are localised or delocalised.

questions.text: Which of the following substituents is a deactivating group (relative to benzene) but still directs an incoming electrophile predominantly to the ortho and para positions?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Classify each substituent by its combined inductive and resonance effect**
\( -NH_2 \) and \( -CH_3 \) are both activating, ortho/para-directing groups (by resonance donation and hyperconjugation respectively); \( -NO_2 \) is a deactivating, meta-directing group (strong -I and -M withdrawal).

**Step 2: Analyse the special case of halogens**
Halogens have a strong electron-withdrawing inductive (-I) effect due to high electronegativity, which dominates and makes the ring less reactive overall (deactivating); however, their lone pairs can still donate into the ring by resonance (+M), and this resonance donation specifically stabilises the arenium ion intermediate only when the electrophile attacks ortho or para to the halogen.

**Step 3: Reconcile the two competing effects**
Because the -I effect controls the overall rate (making halobenzenes react slower than benzene) while the +M effect controls the position (favouring ortho/para over meta), halogens end up as the unique category: deactivating overall, yet still ortho/para-directing.

**Final Answer**
Halogens are the classic exception where a deactivating group is nonetheless an ortho/para director, due to the mismatch between which effect controls rate and which controls orientation.
Final answer: C) \( -X \) (halogen, e.g. -Cl, -Br)
questions.tip: Halogens are the one group family where 'deactivating' and 'ortho/para-directing' occur together - every other deactivating group you meet is meta-directing.

questions.text: Which group is both a deactivator of the benzene ring and a meta-director in electrophilic aromatic substitution?
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the general pattern linking activation/deactivation to directing ability**
With the sole exception of the halogens, every activating group (electron-donating by resonance or induction) is an ortho/para director, and every deactivating group (electron-withdrawing by resonance or induction) is a meta director.

**Step 2: Classify each option**
\( -NH_2 \) and \( -OCH_3 \) donate electron density into the ring through resonance (lone pair donation), making them strongly activating, ortho/para-directing groups; \( -CH_3 \) donates weakly through hyperconjugation and induction, also activating and ortho/para-directing.

**Step 3: Identify the meta-directing deactivator**
\( -NO_2 \) strongly withdraws electron density from the ring by both induction and resonance (its own resonance structures pull electron density away from the ring, especially from the ortho/para positions), making it both a strong deactivator and a meta director.

**Final Answer**
Among these four groups, only \( -NO_2 \) both deactivates the ring and directs the incoming electrophile to the meta position.
Final answer: C) \( -NO_2 \)
questions.tip: Memorise the short exception list of meta-directors (-NO2, -CN, -COOH, -SO3H, -CHO, -COR) - every one of them is also deactivating, with no exceptions.

questions.text: Compared to benzene, does anisole (methoxybenzene, \( C_6H_5OCH_3 \)) react faster or slower in electrophilic aromatic substitution, and why?
options: Slower, because oxygen is highly electronegative and withdraws electron density inductively
Faster, because the oxygen lone pair is donated into the ring by resonance (+M effect), increasing electron density especially at the ortho and para positions
At the same rate, since the methoxy group has no net electronic effect
Slower, because the bulky methyl group sterically blocks the ring
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Identify the dominant electronic effect of -OCH3**
While oxygen is electronegative and does withdraw some electron density inductively (-I), one of its lone pairs is also conjugated with the ring's pi system and can be delocalised into it by resonance (+M effect).

**Step 2: Compare the relative magnitudes**
For -OCH3 (and other groups with a directly attached lone pair on an atom bonded to the ring), the +M resonance donation effect is considerably stronger than the -I inductive withdrawal, so the net effect is a significant increase in electron density around the ring.

**Step 3: Connect electron density to reaction rate**
Since electrophilic aromatic substitution requires the ring to act as a nucleophile toward the incoming electrophile, greater ring electron density (especially at ortho/para positions, where the resonance donation is most effective) translates directly into a faster reaction rate compared to unsubstituted benzene.

**Final Answer**
Anisole reacts considerably faster than benzene in electrophilic substitution because resonance donation from the methoxy oxygen dominates over its inductive withdrawal, enriching the ring with electron density.
Final answer: B) Faster, because the oxygen lone pair is donated into the ring by resonance (+M effect), increasing electron density especially at the ortho and para positions
questions.tip: For any group with a lone pair directly on the atom attached to the ring (-OH, -OR, -NH2, -NHR), always expect the resonance (+M) donating effect to dominate over the inductive (-I) withdrawal, making it a strong activator.

questions.text: Nitration of toluene with concentrated \( HNO_3/H_2SO_4 \) gives predominantly which set of products?
options: Mainly ortho- and para-nitrotoluene, with only a small amount of meta-nitrotoluene
Equal amounts of ortho-, meta-, and para-nitrotoluene
Only 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene directly, with no monosubstitution possible
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Classify the directing effect of the methyl group**
The methyl group in toluene is a weak electron donor (via hyperconjugation and a small +I effect), making it an activating, ortho/para-directing group.

**Step 2: Apply this to the arenium ion intermediate stability**
When the electrophile (\( NO_2^+ \)) attacks ortho or para to the methyl group, the resulting arenium ion has a resonance structure placing the positive charge on the ring carbon directly bearing the methyl group, which is specially stabilised by hyperconjugation from the adjacent \( C-H \) bonds of the methyl group; this stabilisation is not available when attack occurs at the meta position.

**Step 3: Conclude the product distribution**
Because the ortho/para intermediates are more stabilised, nitration occurs mainly at those positions, giving predominantly a mixture of ortho- and para-nitrotoluene, with only a minor amount of the meta isomer.

**Final Answer**
Methyl, being an activating, ortho/para-directing group, channels nitration of toluene mainly to the ortho and para positions.
Final answer: B) Mainly ortho- and para-nitrotoluene, with only a small amount of meta-nitrotoluene
questions.tip: For alkyl-substituted benzenes, always predict mainly ortho plus para products (with only trace meta) in electrophilic substitution.

questions.text: Further nitration of nitrobenzene (to give a dinitrobenzene) occurs predominantly at which ring position, and why?
options: Ortho, because -NO2 is an ortho/para director
Para, because it is furthest from the existing -NO2 group

Meta, because placing the second -NO2 group there avoids putting positive charge on a carbon directly bearing or adjacent to the first strongly electron-withdrawing -NO2 group in the arenium ion intermediate
Ipso (same carbon), by direct displacement of the first -NO2 group
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the electronic nature of the existing -NO2 group**
The nitro group already on the ring is strongly electron-withdrawing by both induction and resonance, pulling electron density away from the ring, and especially away from the ortho and para positions relative to itself.

**Step 2: Compare arenium ion intermediates for attack at each position**
If the second electrophile attacked ortho or para to the existing -NO2 group, one of the resonance structures of the resulting arenium ion would place the new positive charge directly on (or immediately next to) the carbon bearing the powerfully electron-withdrawing nitro group, which is highly destabilising.

**Step 3: Identify the favoured position**
Attack at the meta position avoids ever placing positive charge on the carbon bearing -NO2 in any resonance structure of the intermediate, making the meta pathway comparatively (though still difficult, since the ring overall is deactivated and reaction is slow) the least unfavourable.

**Final Answer**
The strongly deactivating nitro group directs further substitution to the meta position specifically to avoid destabilising positive-charge buildup next to itself.
Final answer: C) Meta, because placing the second -NO2 group there avoids putting positive charge on a carbon directly bearing or adjacent to the first strongly electron-withdrawing -NO2 group in the arenium ion intermediate
questions.tip: For any meta-director, justify the meta preference by explicitly showing that ortho/para attack would place a resonance positive charge right next to the electron-withdrawing group - this is the reasoning examiners look for.

questions.text: In p-nitrotoluene (1-methyl-4-nitrobenzene), bromination is carried out. At which ring position does bromination occur, and which substituent's directing effect controls this outcome?
options: Position 3 (meta to both groups), since both groups oppose each other there

Positions 2 and 6 (ortho to the methyl group and simultaneously meta to the nitro group), since both directing effects reinforce at this position, and the more strongly activating methyl group dominates
Position 5, ortho to the nitro group only
No reaction occurs, since the two directing effects exactly cancel
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Map the directing preferences of each group separately**
With methyl at \( C1 \) and nitro at \( C4 \), the methyl group (an activating ortho/para director) favours attack at \( C2 \), \( C6 \) (ortho to itself) or \( C4 \) (para to itself, already occupied); the nitro group (a deactivating meta director) favours attack at \( C2 \) and \( C6 \) (meta to itself).

**Step 2: Identify where the two preferences coincide**
Both the methyl group's preference (ortho to itself) and the nitro group's preference (meta to itself) point to the same positions, \( C2 \) and \( C6 \), so there is no real conflict between the two directing effects in this particular substitution pattern.

**Step 3: Confirm which group controls the overall rate**
Although both groups agree on position, it is the strongly activating methyl group that makes the ring reactive enough to undergo substitution at all (the electron-poor nitro group alone would make the ring far less reactive), so methyl is considered the dominant, rate-controlling director here.

**Final Answer**
Because the ortho/para-directing methyl group and the meta-directing nitro group reinforce at the same position in p-nitrotoluene, bromination cleanly occurs at \( C2 \)/\( C6 \), controlled predominantly by the activating methyl group.
Final answer: B) Positions 2 and 6 (ortho to the methyl group and simultaneously meta to the nitro group), since both directing effects reinforce at this position, and the more strongly activating methyl group dominates
questions.tip: When two substituents are already present, always check whether their individually predicted positions coincide (reinforcing) or conflict before deciding the major product; when they conflict, the stronger activator usually wins.

questions.text: Nitration of tert-butylbenzene gives predominantly the para-nitro product, with very little ortho product, even though the tert-butyl group is an ortho/para-directing activator. What best explains the low amount of ortho product?
options: The tert-butyl group is actually a meta director

Steric hindrance from the bulky tert-butyl group blocks the electrophile's approach to the adjacent ortho positions, so despite being an activating o,p-director electronically, the para position is favoured for steric reasons
Ortho substitution is electronically forbidden for all alkylbenzenes
The nitronium ion cannot reach any position on a substituted ring
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Confirm the electronic directing effect first**
The tert-butyl group, like other alkyl groups, is electron-donating (by hyperconjugation and induction) and is therefore, on purely electronic grounds, an activating ortho/para director - so both ortho and para positions are electronically favoured over meta.

**Step 2: Recognise the added steric factor**
The tert-butyl group is exceptionally bulky (three methyl groups on the attached carbon), and any electrophile approaching an ortho position experiences significant steric clash with this bulky substituent, raising the energy of that transition state.

**Step 3: Compare with the para position**
The para position is far away from the bulky substituent and experiences no such steric hindrance, so even though both ortho and para are electronically activated to a similar degree, the para pathway is much less hindered and therefore dominates.

**Final Answer**
When a directing group is very bulky, steric hindrance can override the usual near-equal electronic preference for ortho versus para, pushing the product distribution strongly toward para.
Final answer: B) Steric hindrance from the bulky tert-butyl group blocks the electrophile's approach to the adjacent ortho positions, so despite being an activating o,p-director electronically, the para position is favoured for steric reasons
questions.tip: Whenever the directing substituent is bulky (tert-butyl, and similar), expect the para product to dominate heavily over ortho due to steric hindrance, even though both are electronically allowed.

questions.text: Explain why halogens (for example, -Cl) are ortho/para-directing in electrophilic aromatic substitution, yet still deactivate the benzene ring toward the reaction.
options: Halogens have no lone pairs, so they can only withdraw electron density inductively

The halogen lone pair is donated into the ring by resonance (+M), specifically stabilising the arenium ion at ortho/para positions (hence o,p-directing); but the halogen's high electronegativity withdraws electron density inductively (-I) from the whole ring, and since -I dominates over +M in overall magnitude, the ring is net deactivated
Halogens direct meta because they are too electronegative
The deactivation is purely steric, unrelated to electronic effects
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Identify the two competing electronic effects of a halogen substituent**
A halogen atom bonded to the ring has both an inductive effect (strong electron withdrawal, -I, due to high electronegativity) and a resonance effect (donation of one lone pair into the ring's pi system, +M), and these two effects act in opposite directions.

**Step 2: Explain the directing (positional) consequence of the resonance effect**
The +M resonance donation can only stabilise the arenium ion intermediate when the electrophile attacks ortho or para to the halogen (only then can a resonance structure place the halogen's positive character adjacent to its own lone pair donation), so halogens direct incoming electrophiles to those positions.

**Step 3: Explain the rate (reactivity) consequence of the inductive effect**
However, considered over the whole ring and compared to benzene, the halogen's strong electron-withdrawing induction effect outweighs its resonance donation in overall magnitude, so the ring as a whole ends up less electron-rich (and therefore less reactive, i.e. deactivated) than benzene itself.

**Final Answer**
Halogens are the textbook example where the effect controlling reaction rate (net inductive withdrawal, causing deactivation) is different from the effect controlling positional selectivity (resonance donation, causing ortho/para direction).
Final answer: B) The halogen lone pair is donated into the ring by resonance (+M), specifically stabilising the arenium ion at ortho/para positions (hence o,p-directing); but the halogen's high electronegativity withdraws electron density inductively (-I) from the whole ring, and since -I dominates over +M in overall magnitude, the ring is net deactivated
questions.tip: For halogens, keep two separate judgments in mind: -I effect decides the rate (deactivating), +M effect decides the position (ortho/para) - do not conflate the two.

questions.text: Arrange phenol, toluene, benzene, chlorobenzene, and nitrobenzene in decreasing order of reactivity toward electrophilic aromatic substitution.
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Classify each substituent's net electronic effect relative to benzene**
Phenol's -OH is a strong net activator (resonance donation dominates strongly over induction); toluene's -CH3 is a mild net activator (hyperconjugation and weak +I, no competing withdrawal); chlorobenzene's -Cl is a net mild deactivator (its -I withdrawal outweighs its +M donation, though only modestly); nitrobenzene's -NO2 is a strong net deactivator (both -I and -M withdraw strongly, with no compensating donation).

**Step 2: Rank the two activators against benzene itself**
Since -OH donates much more strongly by resonance than the weak hyperconjugative donation of -CH3, phenol is more activated (more reactive) than toluene, and both are more reactive than plain benzene.

**Step 3: Rank the two deactivators against benzene itself**
Chlorobenzene is only mildly deactivated (net -I effect is partly offset by some +M donation), while nitrobenzene is very strongly deactivated (both effects withdraw electron density with no offsetting donation), so chlorobenzene remains more reactive than nitrobenzene, but both are less reactive than benzene.

**Final Answer**
Combining both comparisons gives the overall reactivity order phenol (most activated) down to nitrobenzene (most deactivated), with benzene itself in the middle.
Final answer: B) Phenol > toluene > benzene > chlorobenzene > nitrobenzene
questions.tip: Build reactivity-order questions in two halves: rank all activators against benzene first, then rank all deactivators against benzene, then merge the two lists around benzene in the middle.

questions.text: To synthesise 1,3,5-tribromobenzene (three bromine atoms mutually meta to one another) starting from benzene, chemists use a multi-step route via aniline (nitration, reduction to -NH2, exhaustive bromination, diazotization, then reduction of the diazonium salt with \( H_3PO_2 \) to remove nitrogen) rather than simply treating benzene directly with excess bromine. Why does direct bromination of benzene fail to give this product?
options: Because bromine does not react with benzene at all without a catalyst

Because bromine is an ortho/para director, so successive brominations would keep directing new bromine atoms ortho/para to existing ones, never placing three bromines in a mutually meta (1,3,5) arrangement
Because benzene can only ever hold a maximum of two bromine substituents
Because direct bromination always gives exclusively the 1,2,3-isomer
questions.answer:
**Step 1: Recall the directing effect of bromine already on the ring**
Bromine, though it deactivates the ring, is an ortho/para director (its resonance lone-pair donation stabilises the arenium ion specifically at those positions), so once one bromine is installed on benzene, any further bromination is directed ortho or para to it, never meta.

**Step 2: Trace the consequence through repeated brominations**
Starting from bromobenzene, a second bromination goes ortho/para to the first bromine (never meta), and a third bromination would again be directed ortho/para to the existing bromines - this self-reinforcing ortho/para preference can never produce the alternating, all-meta (1,3,5) substitution pattern directly.

**Step 3: Explain why the aniline route succeeds instead**
The strongly activating -NH2 group in aniline is also an ortho/para director, so exhaustive bromination readily installs three bromines all ortho/para to -NH2, which corresponds to the 2,4,6-positions relative to the amino group; removing the -NH2 group afterward (via diazotization and reduction with \( H_3PO_2 \), replacing -N2+ with -H) leaves three bromine atoms that are now mutually meta (1,3,5) to each other, since their original relationship was set relative to the (now removed) directing group rather than to each other directly.

**Final Answer**
Direct bromination can never give the 1,3,5-pattern because bromine is an ortho/para (never meta) director; the aniline route works by using a strong o,p-director to place the bromines, then removing that director afterward, revealing a net meta relationship among the three bromines.
Final answer: B) Because bromine is an ortho/para director, so successive brominations would keep directing new bromine atoms ortho/para to existing ones, never placing three bromines in a mutually meta (1,3,5) arrangement
questions.tip: For 1,3,5-trisubstitution synthesis problems with only o,p-directing groups available directly, always think of the 'install via a strong o,p-director then remove the director' strategy (commonly via aniline and diazonium chemistry).
